---
title: "Statistical Inference"
---

Every indirect treatment comparison reduces, in the end, to a statement about numbers we estimated from
finite data and the uncertainty attached to them. A network meta-analysis combines log odds ratios, each
of which is a nonlinear function of fitted model parameters; its credible or confidence intervals come
from the curvature of a likelihood. A matching-adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC, [Notation](/notation.qmd)) solves
a system of weighting equations and then reports a standard error that must remain valid even though the
weighting model is almost certainly misspecified. Multilevel network meta-regression fits a likelihood
over individual and aggregate data and inverts the Fisher information to quantify precision. None of
these methods can be stated, let alone trusted, without the machinery of estimation theory: what an
estimator is, when it is unbiased, how its variance behaves, what the likelihood and the score and the
Fisher information are, and how an estimator behaves as the sample grows.

This chapter builds that machinery from first principles. We define statistical models and estimators
and the three numbers that summarize an estimator's accuracy (bias, variance, mean squared error). We
introduce the likelihood, the score function, and the Fisher information, and prove the *information
equality* that ties them together. We define the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE), prove its
functional invariance, and then prove the two results on which all asymptotic inference rests: the MLE
is *consistent* and *asymptotically normal*. We prove the Cramér-Rao lower bound, which says no unbiased
estimator can beat the inverse Fisher information, and we show the MLE attains it asymptotically. We
prove the three asymptotic tools used throughout the book: the continuous mapping theorem, Slutsky's
theorem, and the delta method (catalogue results A.13, A.12, A.11). We then generalize from maximum
likelihood to *M-estimation* and define the *sandwich variance estimator*, the robust standard error
that Chapter 18 needs for MAIC. We close with the Wald, score, and likelihood-ratio tests and the
confidence intervals obtained by inverting them.

Throughout, the data are $X_1, \dots, X_n$, modeled as independent and identically distributed (iid)
draws from a distribution indexed by a parameter $\boldsymbol\theta$. The reader should keep one picture
in mind: the log-likelihood is a random function of $\boldsymbol\theta$; its slope (the score) vanishes
at the MLE; its curvature (the information) determines how sharply the data pin down the parameter; and
asymptotic normality is the statement that, viewed through a magnifying glass of width $1/\sqrt n$, this
random function looks like a parabola whose vertex is Gaussian.

That picture, drawn once, is worth carrying through the whole chapter:

```
   l_n(theta)   (the log-likelihood: how well a value of theta fits the data)
       ^
       |                 _______
       |               /    |    \      <-- peak at theta_hat, the MLE:
       |              /     |     \          the SLOPE here is zero (the score)
       |             /      |      \
       |            /       |       \    <-- the CURVATURE here is the information:
       |          _/        |        \_      a sharper peak means more information
       |       __/          |          \__     and a smaller standard error
       +--------------------+-------------------> theta
                         theta_hat
```

Everything that follows attaches a name and a theorem to one feature of this curve. The table below is a
preview and a reference: each row is defined precisely in the section listed, and you can return to it
whenever a symbol feels unfamiliar.

| Quantity | Symbol | Plain meaning | Defined in |
|---|---|---|---|
| Log-likelihood | $\ell_n(\boldsymbol\theta)$ | how well a parameter value fits the observed data | @def-likelihood |
| Score | $\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta)$ | the slope of the log-likelihood; zero at the MLE | @def-score |
| MLE | $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$ | the parameter value that fits the data best | @def-mle |
| Per-observation information | $\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)$ | how much one observation tells you about $\boldsymbol\theta$ (curvature per data point) | @def-fisher-information |
| Sample information | $\mathcal I_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = n\,\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)$ | how much the whole sample tells you | @cor-information-additivity |
| Observed information | $\mathbf J_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)$ | the actual curvature at the estimate (what software inverts) | @sec-asymptotic-normality |
| Inverse information | $\mathcal I_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)^{-1}$ | approximate variance of the MLE; its square root is the standard error | @thm-mle-asymptotic-normality |

A word on the data. We write the observations as $X_1, \dots, X_n$, but a single $X_i$ can be many things
depending on the model: one yes/no outcome (did patient $i$ respond?), a covariate vector (age, sex,
biomarker), or an entire patient record (covariates, treatment arm, and outcome together). The theory
below never cares which; it only needs the $X_i$ to be iid draws from $f(\cdot\,;\boldsymbol\theta_0)$.

## Statistical models, estimators, and risk {#sec-models}

We work on a probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal F, P)$ in the sense of @def-probability-space. A
*statistical model* is a family of candidate distributions for the data, indexed by a parameter.

::: {#exm-running-trial}
## A running example: a two-arm trial and an indirect comparison
We return to one concrete study at every step. A randomized trial of a new treatment records, for each of
$n = 25$ patients, whether the patient responded ($X_i = 1$) or not ($X_i = 0$):

| Patient $i$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | $\cdots$ | 24 | 25 | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Response $X_i$ | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | $\cdots$ | 1 | 0 | $\sum_i X_i = 10$ |

Ten of the $25$ patients respond. The single number we want is the response probability $p$, together
with an honest measure of how uncertain our estimate of $p$ is. Every tool in this chapter is, in the
end, a way to answer one of two questions about this trial: *what is our best guess for $p$?*
(estimation) and *how far off could that guess be?* (uncertainty).

The destination is an *indirect treatment comparison*. Imagine a second trial of a different treatment
against the same control, reporting its own response probabilities. Neither trial compares the two new
treatments head to head, yet we will want the contrast between them on the log-odds scale, with a valid
standard error. By the end we assemble exactly that (@exm-indirect-bucher), using the likelihood to
estimate each $p$, the Fisher information for its precision, and the delta method to move to the log-odds
scale and combine the two trials. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#def-statistical-model}
## Parametric statistical model
Let $\mathcal X$ be a sample space carrying a $\sigma$-finite dominating measure $\nu$ (Lebesgue measure
for continuous data, counting measure for discrete data). A *parametric statistical model* is a family
$$
\mathcal F = \bigl\{\, f(\cdot\,;\boldsymbol\theta) : \boldsymbol\theta \in \Theta \,\bigr\},
\qquad \Theta \subseteq \mathbb R^{p},
$$
where each $f(\cdot\,;\boldsymbol\theta)$ is a probability density (or mass) function with respect to
$\nu$. The set $\Theta$ is the *parameter space*. The model is *identifiable* if the map
$\boldsymbol\theta \mapsto f(\cdot\,;\boldsymbol\theta)$ is injective, that is, if
$\boldsymbol\theta \ne \boldsymbol\theta'$ implies $f(\cdot\,;\boldsymbol\theta) \ne
f(\cdot\,;\boldsymbol\theta')$ on a set of positive $\nu$-measure.

We observe $X_1, \dots, X_n$ iid with common density $f(\cdot\,;\boldsymbol\theta_0)$ for some unknown
*true parameter* $\boldsymbol\theta_0 \in \Theta$, and write $\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}$,
$\mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}$, $P_{\boldsymbol\theta}$ for expectation, variance, and probability
computed under $f(\cdot\,;\boldsymbol\theta)$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** A statistical model is a *menu of candidate distributions* for the data, one for
each value of $\boldsymbol\theta$; estimation is the job of picking the menu item that best matches what
we saw. Two pieces of jargon in the definition:

- A *$\sigma$-finite dominating measure* $\nu$ is just a fixed reference yardstick that lets the word
"density" mean something. For continuous data it is ordinary length or area (Lebesgue measure), so a
density is the height of a curve; for discrete data it is counting measure, so a "density" is simply a
probability mass $P(X = x)$. You never have to choose $\nu$ in practice: it is Lebesgue for continuous
outcomes and counting for counts or yes/no data.
- *Identifiable* says the map $\boldsymbol\theta \mapsto f(\cdot\,;\boldsymbol\theta)$ is *injective*
(different inputs give different outputs): no two parameter values produce the same distribution of
observable data. If two did, no amount of data could ever tell them apart. For a non-identifiable
example, suppose a model only ever affects the data through a product $\mu = \alpha\beta$ but carries
$\alpha$ and $\beta$ separately; then $(\alpha,\beta) = (2,3)$ and $(6,1)$ give identical data
distributions and are indistinguishable.

A note on $\boldsymbol\theta_0$. Calling it the *true parameter* assumes the model is correctly
specified, that the data really were generated by some member of the menu. Real outcome models are
usually simplifications. We keep the clean "true parameter" language while developing maximum likelihood,
and in @sec-m-estimation we drop it: there the target becomes whatever parameter our estimating equation
aims at, whether or not any menu item is exactly right. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#def-estimator}
## Estimator, bias, variance, mean squared error
An *estimator* of a quantity $g(\boldsymbol\theta) \in \mathbb R$ is a measurable function
$T_n = T(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ of the data alone (it may not depend on $\boldsymbol\theta$). Its *bias*,
*variance*, and *mean squared error* (MSE) at $\boldsymbol\theta$ are
$$
\mathrm{Bias}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T_n) = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[T_n] - g(\boldsymbol\theta),
\qquad
\mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T_n),
\qquad
\mathrm{MSE}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T_n) = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\!\bigl[(T_n - g(\boldsymbol\theta))^2\bigr].
$$
The estimator is *unbiased* if $\mathrm{Bias}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T_n) = 0$ for every
$\boldsymbol\theta \in \Theta$. For a vector estimator $\mathbf T_n$ of
$g(\boldsymbol\theta) \in \mathbb R^q$, the variance is replaced by the covariance matrix
$\mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf T_n)$ and the MSE by the matrix
$\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[(\mathbf T_n - g)(\mathbf T_n - g)^\top]$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** An estimator is a *recipe* that turns the data into a guess, with no peeking at
the unknown $\boldsymbol\theta$. In the running example the obvious estimator of $p$ is the sample
proportion $\hat p = \tfrac1n\sum_i X_i = 10/25 = 0.40$. *Bias* is the systematic part of the error (does
the recipe aim at the right target on average?), *variance* is the random scatter from sample to sample,
and *mean squared error* combines the two. These three numbers are exactly how competing estimators are
graded in the simulation studies of Chapter 29. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The bias and the variance measure two different failures: bias is a systematic offset, variance is
random scatter. The MSE combines them, and the decomposition below shows exactly how.

::: {#prp-bias-variance-decomposition}
## Bias-variance decomposition
For any estimator $T_n$ with $\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[T_n^2] < \infty$,
$$
\mathrm{MSE}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T_n)
= \mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T_n) + \bigl(\mathrm{Bias}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T_n)\bigr)^2 .
$$ {#eq-bias-variance}
For a vector estimator $\mathbf T_n$ of $g(\boldsymbol\theta)\in\mathbb R^q$, the matrix MSE equals
$\mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf T_n) + \mathbf b\,\mathbf b^\top$ with
$\mathbf b = \mathrm{Bias}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf T_n)$, and taking traces gives the scalar
identity $\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\|\mathbf T_n - g\|_2^2 = \mathrm{tr}\,\mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf T_n) + \|\mathbf b\|_2^2$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $m = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[T_n]$ and $b = m - g(\boldsymbol\theta)$. Then
$$
\mathrm{MSE}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T_n)
= \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\bigl[(T_n - m + b)^2\bigr]
= \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\bigl[(T_n - m)^2\bigr] + 2 b\, \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[T_n - m] + b^2 .
$$
The cross term vanishes because $\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[T_n - m] = 0$, and the first term is
$\mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T_n)$ by definition, giving @eq-bias-variance. The vector statement is
identical with $\mathbf m = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[\mathbf T_n]$ and
$\mathbf b = \mathbf m - g$: expand
$(\mathbf T_n - g)(\mathbf T_n - g)^\top = (\mathbf T_n - \mathbf m)(\mathbf T_n - \mathbf m)^\top + (\mathbf T_n - \mathbf m)\mathbf b^\top + \mathbf b(\mathbf T_n - \mathbf m)^\top + \mathbf b\mathbf b^\top$
and take $\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}$; the two middle terms vanish. The trace identity follows from
$\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf b\mathbf b^\top) = \|\mathbf b\|_2^2$ and linearity of the trace. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters.** The decomposition is the rule for trading bias against variance. A more complicated
adjustment model (more covariates in a regression, a more flexible weighting model in MAIC) usually
lowers bias but raises variance; @eq-bias-variance is the scoreboard on which that trade is settled, and
it is why a slightly biased estimator can be the more accurate one (@exr-mse-shrinkage). $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

Two notions of "the estimator gets it right as data accumulate" recur throughout the book. The first is
asymptotic and concerns a *sequence* of estimators.

::: {#def-consistent-estimator}
## Consistency
A sequence of estimators $T_n$ is *(weakly) consistent* for $g(\boldsymbol\theta_0)$ if
$T_n \xrightarrow{p} g(\boldsymbol\theta_0)$ as $n \to \infty$, that is, for every $\varepsilon > 0$,
$P_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}\!\bigl(|T_n - g(\boldsymbol\theta_0)| > \varepsilon\bigr) \to 0$. It is *strongly
consistent* if $T_n \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} g(\boldsymbol\theta_0)$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** Consistency is the promise that *with enough data the estimator lands on the
truth*. Weak consistency (convergence in probability) is all we use in this book; strong consistency
(almost-sure convergence, from Chapter 4) is the stronger statement that the estimator settles down for
almost every possible infinite data stream, not merely with high probability at each $n$. For the running
example, consistency is the guarantee that $\hat p \to p$ as the trial grows; in later chapters it is the
guarantee that network meta-analysis and MAIC estimates stop being systematically wrong as studies get
larger. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
Unbiasedness and consistency are logically independent. The sample mean $\bar X_n$ of iid data with mean
$\mu$ and finite variance is both unbiased ($\mathbb E[\bar X_n] = \mu$) and consistent (by the weak law
of large numbers below). But $T_n = X_1$ is unbiased for $\mu$ yet not consistent, and a biased
estimator whose bias and variance both vanish (for example a shrunken mean
$\tfrac{n}{n+1}\bar X_n$) is consistent: its bias is
$\tfrac{n}{n+1}\mu - \mu = -\mu/(n+1) \to 0$ and its variance is
$\bigl(\tfrac{n}{n+1}\bigr)^2 \sigma^2/n \to 0$, so by @eq-bias-variance its MSE vanishes. The MSE in @eq-bias-variance is the right single-number summary
of finite-sample accuracy, because $\mathrm{MSE}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T_n)\to 0$ is equivalent to
$L^2$ convergence, which implies consistency by Chebyshev's inequality. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Asymptotic tools: continuous mapping, Slutsky, and the delta method {#sec-asymptotic-tools}

**Why this section, and why now.** Here is the concrete problem these three tools solve. In the running
example we will estimate $p$, but a network meta-analysis never reports a probability; it reports a *log
odds ratio*, a nonlinear function of fitted probabilities. So the real question is: given the uncertainty
in $\hat p$, what is the uncertainty in $\log\frac{\hat p}{1 - \hat p}$, or in a contrast of two such
quantities across trials? The *delta method* below is the machine that answers this, and it is the single
most-used result of the chapter, because every effect measure in the book (log odds ratio, log hazard
ratio, risk difference) is a smooth function of fitted parameters. The continuous mapping theorem and
Slutsky's theorem are the two lemmas the delta method (and the later limit theory of the MLE) is built
from. If you read this section for one thing, read it for the delta method and @exm-indirect-bucher. One
honest word about ordering: we prove these tools before we have an estimator in hand because the
consistency and normality proofs will call them repeatedly; keep the running example's $\hat p$ in mind as
the thing they will eventually be applied to.

Before we can analyze any estimator as $n \to \infty$ we need three theorems about how limits in
distribution interact with continuous functions and with constants. We will use them constantly, so we
prove them here, near the front. We take as given two classical results from probability, which belong
to the foundations of Chapter 4 and which we cite rather than reprove; see @bingham2010regression and a
standard graduate probability text for proofs.

::: {.remark}
## Prerequisites cited from probability
We use the following standard facts about iid random vectors $X_1, X_2, \dots$ in $\mathbb R^p$.

1. **Weak law of large numbers (WLLN).** If $\mathbb E\|X_1\| < \infty$ with mean $\boldsymbol\mu$, then
$\bar X_n = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\mu$.

2. **Multivariate central limit theorem (CLT).** If, in addition, $X_1$ has finite covariance matrix
$\boldsymbol\Sigma$, then $\sqrt n\,(\bar X_n - \boldsymbol\mu) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N_p(\mathbf 0, \boldsymbol\Sigma)$.

3. **Portmanteau theorem.** $X_n \xrightarrow{d} X$ if and only if
$\mathbb E[h(X_n)] \to \mathbb E[h(X)]$ for every bounded continuous $h$; equivalently, if and only if
$\mathbb E[h(X_n)] \to \mathbb E[h(X)]$ for every bounded function $h$ that is continuous at
$P_X$-almost every point.

4. **Cramér-Wold device.** $X_n \xrightarrow{d} X$ in $\mathbb R^p$ if and only if
$\mathbf t^\top X_n \xrightarrow{d} \mathbf t^\top X$ in $\mathbb R$ for every $\mathbf t \in \mathbb R^p$.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
## The $O_p$ and $o_p$ shorthand (read once, use everywhere)
Two of the proofs below use a compact notation for "stochastically small" and "stochastically bounded,"
listed in [Notation](/notation.qmd). A sequence of random vectors $V_n$ is $o_p(1)$ if
$V_n \xrightarrow{p} \mathbf 0$ (it vanishes), and $O_p(1)$ if it is *bounded in probability*: for every
$\varepsilon > 0$ there is a constant $K$ with $\sup_n P(\|V_n\| > K) < \varepsilon$ (it does not run off
to infinity). Three rules are all we need, and each is elementary:

1. A sequence that converges in distribution is $O_p(1)$ (a convergent limit law cannot put mass at
infinity).
2. $o_p(1) \times O_p(1) = o_p(1)$: something vanishing times something bounded vanishes.
3. $o_p(1) + o_p(1) = o_p(1)$ and $O_p(1) + O_p(1) = O_p(1)$.

These are exactly the steps that let us discard remainder terms in the delta method and in Wilks'
theorem. You do not need their proofs to follow the chapter; treat them as arithmetic for random
sequences. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The first tool says continuous functions preserve convergence in distribution. It corresponds to A.13 in
the proof catalogue.

::: {#thm-continuous-mapping}
## Continuous mapping theorem
Let $X_n, X$ be random vectors in $\mathbb R^p$ and let $g : \mathbb R^p \to \mathbb R^q$ be measurable.
Let $D_g$ be the set of discontinuity points of $g$ and suppose $P(X \in D_g) = 0$. Then:

(i) $X_n \xrightarrow{d} X \;\Rightarrow\; g(X_n) \xrightarrow{d} g(X)$;

(ii) $X_n \xrightarrow{p} X \;\Rightarrow\; g(X_n) \xrightarrow{p} g(X)$;

(iii) $X_n \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} X \;\Rightarrow\; g(X_n) \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} g(X)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
*(i)* Let $h : \mathbb R^q \to \mathbb R$ be bounded and continuous. The composition $h \circ g$ is
bounded by $\|h\|_\infty$, and it is continuous at every point where $g$ is continuous, hence at every
point of $\mathbb R^p \setminus D_g$, a set of $P_X$-probability one. By the second (almost-everywhere)
form of the Portmanteau theorem, $\mathbb E[h(g(X_n))] = \mathbb E[(h\circ g)(X_n)] \to \mathbb E[(h\circ g)(X)] = \mathbb E[h(g(X))]$.
As $h$ was an arbitrary bounded continuous function, the first form of Portmanteau gives
$g(X_n) \xrightarrow{d} g(X)$.

*(iii)* If $X_n(\omega) \to X(\omega)$ and $X(\omega) \notin D_g$, then $g(X_n(\omega)) \to g(X(\omega))$
by continuity of $g$ at $X(\omega)$. This holds for all $\omega$ outside the union of the
null set $\{X_n \not\to X\}$ and the null set $\{X \in D_g\}$, which is null; hence
$g(X_n) \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} g(X)$.

*(ii)* Suppose $g(X_n) \overset{p}{\nrightarrow} g(X)$. Then there exist $\varepsilon, \eta > 0$ and a
subsequence along which $P(\|g(X_n) - g(X)\| > \varepsilon) > \eta$. Along that subsequence
$X_n \xrightarrow{p} X$ still holds, so it has a further subsequence with
$X_{n_k} \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} X$ (a standard fact: convergence in probability implies almost-sure
convergence along a subsequence; see @bingham2010regression). Intuitively, a sequence converges in
probability if and only if every subsequence contains a further subsequence that converges almost surely,
and the contradiction we now derive exploits exactly that escape hatch. By part (iii),
$g(X_{n_k}) \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} g(X)$, hence $g(X_{n_k}) \xrightarrow{p} g(X)$, contradicting
$P(\|g(X_{n_k}) - g(X)\| > \varepsilon) > \eta$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters.** This is the "plug-in" theorem: if an estimate converges, a continuous
transformation of it converges too. It is what lets us pass from a converging $\hat p$ to a converging
odds $\hat p/(1 - \hat p)$, or from a converging log odds ratio to its converging exponential, the odds
ratio. One-line example: if $\bar X_n \xrightarrow{p} \mu$ then $\bar X_n^2 \xrightarrow{p} \mu^2$. What
to remember: continuity transfers convergence, provided the function is well behaved at the limit.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The second tool lets us combine a sequence that converges in distribution with one that converges to a
constant. It corresponds to A.12.

::: {#thm-slutsky}
## Slutsky's theorem
Let $X_n \xrightarrow{d} X$ in $\mathbb R^p$ and let $Y_n \xrightarrow{p} \mathbf c$ for a constant
$\mathbf c \in \mathbb R^p$ (respectively a constant matrix $C_n \xrightarrow{p} C$). Then
$$
X_n + Y_n \xrightarrow{d} X + \mathbf c,
\qquad
Y_n^\top X_n \xrightarrow{d} \mathbf c^\top X,
\qquad
C_n X_n \xrightarrow{d} C\,X .
$$
If $p = 1$ and $\mathbf c \ne 0$, then $X_n / Y_n \xrightarrow{d} X/\mathbf c$.
:::

::: {.proof}
The key step is that joint convergence holds: $(X_n, Y_n) \xrightarrow{d} (X, \mathbf c)$ in
$\mathbb R^{2p}$. To see this, take a bounded uniformly continuous $h:\mathbb R^{2p}\to\mathbb R$ with
modulus of continuity $\omega_h(\delta) = \sup\{|h(u)-h(v)| : \|u-v\|\le\delta\}$, which satisfies
$\omega_h(\delta) \to 0$ as $\delta \downarrow 0$. For any $\delta > 0$,
$$
\bigl|\mathbb E[h(X_n, Y_n)] - \mathbb E[h(X_n, \mathbf c)]\bigr|
\le \omega_h(\delta) + 2\|h\|_\infty\, P(\|Y_n - \mathbf c\| > \delta).
$$
This inequality splits the difference by where $Y_n$ lands. On the good event
$\{\|Y_n - \mathbf c\| \le \delta\}$ the two points $(X_n, Y_n)$ and $(X_n, \mathbf c)$ are within
$\delta$ of each other, so $h$ differs between them by at most the modulus $\omega_h(\delta)$. On the bad
event $\{\|Y_n - \mathbf c\| > \delta\}$ we cannot control the difference, but $h$ is bounded by
$\|h\|_\infty$, so the difference is at most $2\|h\|_\infty$, weighted by the probability
$P(\|Y_n - \mathbf c\| > \delta)$ of that event. Letting $n \to \infty$ and using $Y_n \xrightarrow{p} \mathbf c$ kills the last term, leaving
$\limsup_n |\mathbb E[h(X_n, Y_n)] - \mathbb E[h(X_n, \mathbf c)]| \le \omega_h(\delta)$; since
$\delta$ is arbitrary, the limsup is zero. Meanwhile $\mathbb E[h(X_n, \mathbf c)] \to \mathbb E[h(X, \mathbf c)]$
because $u \mapsto h(u, \mathbf c)$ is bounded and continuous and $X_n \xrightarrow d X$. Hence
$\mathbb E[h(X_n, Y_n)] \to \mathbb E[h(X, \mathbf c)]$ for all bounded uniformly continuous $h$, which by
the Portmanteau theorem (uniformly continuous test functions suffice) gives
$(X_n, Y_n) \xrightarrow{d} (X, \mathbf c)$.

Now apply the continuous mapping theorem (@thm-continuous-mapping). The maps
$(x, y) \mapsto x + y$, $(x, y) \mapsto y^\top x$, and (matrix version) $(x, C) \mapsto C x$ are
continuous everywhere, so $X_n + Y_n \xrightarrow{d} X + \mathbf c$, $Y_n^\top X_n \xrightarrow{d} \mathbf c^\top X$,
and $C_n X_n \xrightarrow{d} C X$. The map $(x, y) \mapsto x/y$ is continuous on
$\mathbb R \times (\mathbb R \setminus \{0\})$, and the limit $(X, \mathbf c)$ lands in that set with
probability one when $\mathbf c \ne 0$, so $X_n/Y_n \xrightarrow{d} X/\mathbf c$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters.** Slutsky lets us replace an unknown constant by a consistent estimate without
changing a limiting distribution. This is why a $z$- or $t$-statistic still works when we plug an
*estimated* standard error into the denominator: the numerator has a central limit theorem, the
denominator converges to a constant, and Slutsky glues them. One-line example: if
$\sqrt n(\bar X_n - \mu) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)$ and $S_n \xrightarrow{p} \sigma$, then
$\sqrt n(\bar X_n - \mu)/S_n \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N(0, 1)$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The third tool transfers a $\sqrt n$ central limit theorem through a smooth transformation. It is the
single most-used result of this chapter in later applications, because every effect measure in the book
(log odds ratio, log hazard ratio, risk difference) is a smooth function of fitted parameters. It
corresponds to A.11.

::: {#thm-delta-method}
## Delta method
Let $\mathbf T_n$ be a sequence of $\mathbb R^p$-valued estimators and $\boldsymbol\theta \in \mathbb R^p$
a constant with
$$
\sqrt n\,(\mathbf T_n - \boldsymbol\theta) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N_p(\mathbf 0, \boldsymbol\Sigma).
$$
Let $g : \mathbb R^p \to \mathbb R^q$ be differentiable at $\boldsymbol\theta$ with Jacobian matrix
$\mathbf D = \bigl[\partial g_a / \partial \theta_b\bigr]_{a,b}$ evaluated at $\boldsymbol\theta$. Then
$$
\sqrt n\,\bigl(g(\mathbf T_n) - g(\boldsymbol\theta)\bigr)
\xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N_q\!\bigl(\mathbf 0,\; \mathbf D\,\boldsymbol\Sigma\,\mathbf D^\top\bigr).
$$ {#eq-delta-variance}
In the scalar case $p = q = 1$ this reads
$\sqrt n\,(g(T_n) - g(\theta)) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N\!\bigl(0,\, g'(\theta)^2 \sigma^2\bigr)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
First note that $\sqrt n\,(\mathbf T_n - \boldsymbol\theta) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N_p(\mathbf 0, \boldsymbol\Sigma)$
implies $\mathbf T_n - \boldsymbol\theta = n^{-1/2}\bigl[\sqrt n(\mathbf T_n - \boldsymbol\theta)\bigr] \xrightarrow{p} \mathbf 0$
by Slutsky (@thm-slutsky) with the constant sequence $n^{-1/2} \to 0$; hence
$\mathbf T_n \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta$.

Differentiability of $g$ at $\boldsymbol\theta$ means
$$
g(\mathbf t) = g(\boldsymbol\theta) + \mathbf D\,(\mathbf t - \boldsymbol\theta) + R(\mathbf t),
\qquad
\frac{\|R(\mathbf t)\|}{\|\mathbf t - \boldsymbol\theta\|} \to 0 \ \text{ as } \mathbf t \to \boldsymbol\theta,
$$
with the convention $R(\boldsymbol\theta) = \mathbf 0$. Define the function
$\rho(\mathbf t) = \|R(\mathbf t)\| / \|\mathbf t - \boldsymbol\theta\|$ for
$\mathbf t \ne \boldsymbol\theta$ and $\rho(\boldsymbol\theta) = 0$; then $\rho$ is continuous at
$\boldsymbol\theta$. Multiplying the expansion at $\mathbf t = \mathbf T_n$ by $\sqrt n$,
$$
\sqrt n\,\bigl(g(\mathbf T_n) - g(\boldsymbol\theta)\bigr)
= \mathbf D\,\underbrace{\sqrt n\,(\mathbf T_n - \boldsymbol\theta)}_{=:\,\mathbf Z_n}
\;+\; \sqrt n\, R(\mathbf T_n).
$$
The remainder is controlled by
$\|\sqrt n\,R(\mathbf T_n)\| = \rho(\mathbf T_n)\,\|\mathbf Z_n\|$. Since $\mathbf T_n \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta$
and $\rho$ is continuous at $\boldsymbol\theta$ with $\rho(\boldsymbol\theta) = 0$, the continuous
mapping theorem (@thm-continuous-mapping) gives $\rho(\mathbf T_n) \xrightarrow{p} 0$; and
$\|\mathbf Z_n\| \xrightarrow{d} \|\mathbf Z\|$ where $\mathbf Z \sim \mathcal N_p(\mathbf 0, \boldsymbol\Sigma)$,
so $\|\mathbf Z_n\| = O_p(1)$ (rule 1 of the $O_p/o_p$ remark above: a convergent-in-distribution
sequence is bounded in probability). Hence
$\sqrt n\,R(\mathbf T_n) = \rho(\mathbf T_n)\,\|\mathbf Z_n\| \xrightarrow{p} \mathbf 0$, the product of an
$o_p(1)$ and an $O_p(1)$ sequence (rule 2). Applying Slutsky once more,
$$
\sqrt n\,\bigl(g(\mathbf T_n) - g(\boldsymbol\theta)\bigr)
= \mathbf D\,\mathbf Z_n + o_p(1) \xrightarrow{d} \mathbf D\,\mathbf Z .
$$
Finally $\mathbf D \mathbf Z \sim \mathcal N_q(\mathbf 0, \mathbf D\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf D^\top)$ because
an affine image of a Gaussian is Gaussian with the transformed covariance (@thm-mvn-linear). This is
@eq-delta-variance. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
The hypothesis $g'(\theta) \ne 0$ (more generally, $\mathbf D$ of full row rank) is what makes the limit
*nondegenerate*. If $g'(\theta) = 0$ the first-order term vanishes and the correct rate is $n$ rather
than $\sqrt n$, with a $\chi^2$-type limit driven by the second derivative; this *second-order delta
method* underlies the asymptotics of the likelihood-ratio statistic in @sec-tests.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters.** This is the result that produces a standard error for almost every effect measure
you will report. When you fit a model and then transform a coefficient (a probability into a log odds, a
rate into a log rate, two coefficients into a ratio), the delta-method formula @eq-delta-variance gives
the variance of the transform: multiply the variance of the fitted parameter by the squared derivative
(scalar case), or sandwich the covariance between the Jacobian $\mathbf D$ and its transpose (vector
case). It is the source of the familiar "standard error of a log odds ratio" and, in
@exm-indirect-bucher, of the standard error of an *indirect* comparison. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#exm-delta-logodds}
## Delta method for a log odds (a first taste)
Anticipating the running example, the central limit theorem for a proportion gives
$\sqrt n\,(\hat p - p) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N(0,\, p(1 - p))$. We want the uncertainty of the *log
odds* $g(p) = \log\frac{p}{1 - p}$, whose derivative is $g'(p) = \frac{1}{p(1 - p)}$. The scalar delta
method (@thm-delta-method) gives
$$
\sqrt n\,\bigl(g(\hat p) - g(p)\bigr) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N\!\Bigl(0,\; g'(p)^2\, p(1 - p)\Bigr)
= \mathcal N\!\Bigl(0,\; \tfrac{1}{p(1 - p)}\Bigr),
$$
so $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}\bigl(g(\hat p)\bigr) \approx \frac{1}{n\,\hat p(1 - \hat p)} = \frac{1}{n\hat p} + \frac{1}{n(1 - \hat p)} = \frac{1}{\#\text{responders}} + \frac{1}{\#\text{non-responders}}$.
For our trial ($n = 25$, $10$ responders) this is $\tfrac1{10} + \tfrac1{15} = 0.1\overline 6$, so the log
odds has standard error $\sqrt{0.1\overline 6} = 0.408$. The reading is concrete: a parameter on an
awkward scale (a probability, bounded in $[0,1]$) is moved to a convenient unbounded scale (the log odds)
and its standard error comes along for free. The full computation, with confidence intervals, returns in
@exm-binomial-inference. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#exm-indirect-bucher}
## A toy indirect treatment comparison
Here is the chapter's subject in miniature. Two randomized trials share a common control $A$. Trial 1
compares a new treatment $B$ against $A$; trial 2 compares a different treatment $C$ against $A$. No trial
compares $B$ with $C$, yet we want that contrast on the log-odds-ratio scale.

| Trial | Arm | Responders | Non-responders |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $B$ | 20 | 30 |
| 1 | $A$ | 10 | 40 |
| 2 | $C$ | 18 | 42 |
| 2 | $A$ | 15 | 45 |

Each arm gives a log odds $\log\frac{\hat p}{1 - \hat p}$ whose variance, by @exm-delta-logodds, is
($1/\text{responders} + 1/\text{non-responders}$). A log odds *ratio* is a difference of two independent
arm log odds, so its variance is the sum of the four reciprocals. For the direct contrasts,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat d_{BA} &= \log\tfrac{20/30}{10/40} = \log\tfrac{20\cdot 40}{30\cdot 10} = 0.9808, &
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\widehat d_{BA}) &= \tfrac1{20} + \tfrac1{30} + \tfrac1{10} + \tfrac1{40} = 0.20833,\\
\widehat d_{CA} &= \log\tfrac{18/42}{15/45} = \log\tfrac{18\cdot 45}{42\cdot 15} = 0.2513, &
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\widehat d_{CA}) &= \tfrac1{18} + \tfrac1{42} + \tfrac1{15} + \tfrac1{45} = 0.16825.
\end{aligned}
$$
The indirect contrast of $B$ versus $C$ is the difference
$\widehat d_{BC} = \widehat d_{BA} - \widehat d_{CA} = 0.9808 - 0.2513 = 0.7295$. Because the two trials
are independent, the variances add (there is no covariance term across independent studies in
@eq-delta-variance): $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\widehat d_{BC}) = 0.20833 + 0.16825 = 0.37658$, so the
standard error is $\sqrt{0.37658} = 0.6137$. A 95% interval is
$0.7295 \pm 1.96 \times 0.6137 = (-0.4733,\, 1.9323)$, and on the odds-ratio scale
$(e^{-0.4733}, e^{1.9323}) = (0.62,\, 6.91)$. The interval covers $1$, so the indirect comparison is
inconclusive; and note its standard error ($0.61$) exceeds either direct one ($0.46$ and $0.41$):
combining two estimates *adds* uncertainty. This is the Bucher indirect comparison, developed in full in
Chapter 14; every number above came from the delta method plus the independence of the two trials.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Likelihood, score, and Fisher information {#sec-likelihood}

The likelihood reverses the usual reading of a density. Where $f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)$ is, for fixed
$\boldsymbol\theta$, a function of the data $x$, the likelihood fixes the observed data and varies the
parameter.

::: {#def-likelihood}
## Likelihood and log-likelihood
Given observed data $X_1, \dots, X_n$ from the model @def-statistical-model, the *likelihood function* is
$$
L_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} f(X_i;\boldsymbol\theta),
\qquad \boldsymbol\theta \in \Theta,
$$
viewed as a (random) function of $\boldsymbol\theta$. The *log-likelihood* is
$$
\ell_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \log L_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log f(X_i;\boldsymbol\theta).
$$
For a single observation we write $\ell(\boldsymbol\theta; x) = \log f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)$, so
$\ell_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \sum_i \ell(\boldsymbol\theta; X_i)$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** The likelihood asks, of each candidate $\boldsymbol\theta$, "how probable were
the data we actually saw, if this were the parameter?" High likelihood means good fit. Taking logs turns
the product over independent patients into a sum, which is why every formula below is additive over the
sample. For the running example,
$\ell_n(p) = \bigl(\textstyle\sum_i X_i\bigr)\log p + \bigl(n - \textstyle\sum_i X_i\bigr)\log(1 - p) = 10\log p + 15\log(1 - p)$,
a function of $p$ alone once the data are in hand. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The slope of the log-likelihood in $\boldsymbol\theta$ is the score; the MLE is found by setting it to
zero.

::: {#def-score}
## Score function
The (per-observation) *score* is the gradient of the single-observation log-likelihood in the parameter,
$$
\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; x) = \nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\,\log f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)
= \frac{\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta} f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)}{f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)} \in \mathbb R^{p},
$$
defined wherever $f(x;\boldsymbol\theta) > 0$. The *sample score* is
$$
\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\,\ell_n(\boldsymbol\theta)
= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X_i).
$$ {#eq-score-def}
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** The score $\mathbf s_n$ is the *slope* of the log-likelihood hill in the
parameter ($\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}$ is the gradient, the vector of partial derivatives in each
coordinate of $\boldsymbol\theta$). It points in the direction that would increase the fit, and it is zero
exactly at the top of the hill, the MLE. Read it as "how strongly, and in which direction, the data push
each parameter." We compute the Bernoulli score just below, in @lem-score-mean-zero. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

All of the clean identities about the score require an interchange of differentiation and integration,
which is not automatic. We isolate the needed conditions in one definition and refer back to it.

::: {#def-regular-model}
## Regularity conditions
The model @def-statistical-model is *regular* at an interior point
$\boldsymbol\theta \in \mathrm{int}\,\Theta$ if:

(R1) **Common support.** The set $\{x : f(x;\boldsymbol\theta) > 0\}$ does not depend on
$\boldsymbol\theta$.

(R2) **Smoothness.** For $\nu$-almost every $x$, the map $\boldsymbol\theta \mapsto f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)$
is twice continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of $\boldsymbol\theta$.

(R3) **Differentiation under the integral.** The first two derivatives in $\boldsymbol\theta$ of
$\int f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\,d\nu(x) = 1$ may be taken inside the integral; concretely there are
$\nu$-integrable envelopes dominating $\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta} f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\|$ and
$\|\nabla^2_{\boldsymbol\theta} f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\|$ uniformly in a neighborhood, so the dominated
convergence theorem applies.

(R4) **Finite, positive-definite information.** The Fisher information @def-fisher-information exists,
is finite, and is positive definite at $\boldsymbol\theta$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation: what R1-R4 are for.** These are safety checks that make the log-likelihood smooth
enough, and its tails light enough, for calculus to behave. R1 (common support) says the set of possible
outcomes does not move as $\boldsymbol\theta$ changes: true for the Bernoulli, where outcomes are always
$\{0, 1\}$, but *false* for Uniform$(0,\theta)$, whose range grows with $\theta$ (@exr-information-equality-fail).
R2 (smoothness) says the log-likelihood has a well-defined slope and curvature. R3 (differentiation under
the integral) is the license to swap a derivative with an integral, which is what every score identity
below secretly uses; the "integrable envelopes" are a domination condition that makes the swap legal. R4
(positive-definite information) says no direction of the parameter is left totally undetermined by the
data. Read R1-R4 as "the curve is smooth, its tails are tame, and the parameter is locally pinned down";
the rest is the machinery that turns those words into theorems. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

Under (R1)-(R3) the score has mean zero. This is the cornerstone identity from which everything else
(the information equality, the Cramér-Rao bound, the asymptotics of the MLE) follows.

::: {#lem-score-mean-zero}
## The score has mean zero
If the model is regular (@def-regular-model) at $\boldsymbol\theta$, then
$\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\bigl[\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X)\bigr] = \mathbf 0$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Because $f(\cdot;\boldsymbol\theta)$ integrates to $1$ for every $\boldsymbol\theta$, differentiating the
identity $\int f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\, d\nu(x) = 1$ and moving the gradient inside the integral
(licensed by (R3)),
$$
\mathbf 0 = \nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta} \int f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\, d\nu(x)
= \int \nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta} f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\, d\nu(x)
= \int \frac{\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta} f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)}{f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)}\, f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\, d\nu(x)
= \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\bigl[\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X)\bigr],
$$
where the third equality multiplies and divides by $f$ on the set $\{f > 0\}$, which carries all the
mass by (R1). Condition (R1) is doing real work here: because the support $\{f > 0\}$ does not move with
$\boldsymbol\theta$, differentiating the integral produces no extra term from a $\boldsymbol\theta$-moving
boundary, and the interchange of $\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}$ with the integral is clean. (When the
support *does* move with $\boldsymbol\theta$, as for Uniform$(0,\theta)$ in
@exr-information-equality-fail, this lemma fails.) $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What this means, and the Bernoulli score.** The score is the slope of the log-likelihood. Saying its
average is zero at the truth means: *the true parameter is, on average, the value at which the data give
no reason to nudge the estimate up or down.* That is exactly why the MLE, found by setting the score to
zero, aims at the truth. For the running example the single-observation log-likelihood is
$\ell(p; x) = x\log p + (1 - x)\log(1 - p)$, so the score is
$$
s(p; x) = \frac{x}{p} - \frac{1 - x}{1 - p} = \frac{x - p}{p(1 - p)},
$$
and since $\mathbb E[X] = p$ its mean is $\mathbb E[s(p; X)] = (p - p)/(p(1 - p)) = 0$, confirming
@lem-score-mean-zero. The numerator $x - p$ shows the score is positive when a success pushes the estimate
up and negative when a failure pulls it down. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

Since the score has mean zero, its covariance is just its second moment. That second moment is the
Fisher information.

::: {#def-fisher-information}
## Fisher information
For a regular model the *Fisher information matrix* (in one observation) at $\boldsymbol\theta$ is the
covariance of the score,
$$
\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)
= \mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}\bigl(\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X)\bigr)
= \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\!\bigl[\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X)\,\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X)^\top\bigr]
\in \mathbb R^{p\times p}.
$$ {#eq-fisher-def}
The information in the full sample of size $n$ is
$\mathcal I_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta))$.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** Fisher information measures *how much one observation tells you about*
$\boldsymbol\theta$. There are two equivalent readings, made precise in @thm-information-equality below:
it is the variance of the score (how much the slope of the log-likelihood jumps around from sample to
sample) and it is the average curvature of the log-likelihood (how sharply peaked it is). A sharply peaked
log-likelihood pins down the parameter tightly, so large information means small standard error. For the
Bernoulli, $\mathcal I(p) = 1/[p(1 - p)]$, which is smallest at $p = 1/2$ (a 50/50 outcome is the least
informative) and blows up near $0$ or $1$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

Fisher information is always positive semidefinite (it is a covariance matrix, @thm-cov-psd), and (R4)
asks that it be strictly positive definite, which is the analytic statement that the parameter is
locally identifiable: no nonzero direction leaves the log-likelihood flat in expectation.

::: {#thm-information-equality}
## Information equality
If the model is regular (@def-regular-model) at $\boldsymbol\theta$, then the Fisher information equals
minus the expected Hessian of the log-likelihood:
$$
\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)
= \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\!\bigl[\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X)\,\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X)^\top\bigr]
= -\,\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\!\bigl[\nabla^2_{\boldsymbol\theta}\,\ell(\boldsymbol\theta; X)\bigr].
$$ {#eq-info-equality}
:::

::: {.proof}
The first equality is @eq-fisher-def together with @lem-score-mean-zero (mean-zero makes the second
moment equal the covariance). For the second, start from
$\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; x) = \nabla f / f$ and compute the Hessian of
$\ell(\boldsymbol\theta; x) = \log f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)$ by the quotient rule for gradients (the vector
version of the scalar quotient rule; if it helps, read the display one component of $\boldsymbol\theta$ at
a time, with $\nabla^2$ the Hessian, the matrix of second partial derivatives):
$$
\nabla^2_{\boldsymbol\theta}\,\ell(\boldsymbol\theta; x)
= \nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\!\left(\frac{\nabla f}{f}\right)
= \frac{\nabla^2 f}{f} - \frac{(\nabla f)(\nabla f)^\top}{f^2}
= \frac{\nabla^2 f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)}{f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)} - \mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; x)\,\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; x)^\top,
$$
using $\nabla f / f = \mathbf s$ in the last term. Take $\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}$ of both sides. The
first term integrates to zero:
$$
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\!\left[\frac{\nabla^2 f(X;\boldsymbol\theta)}{f(X;\boldsymbol\theta)}\right]
= \int \frac{\nabla^2 f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)}{f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)}\, f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\, d\nu(x)
= \int \nabla^2 f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\, d\nu(x)
= \nabla^2 \int f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\, d\nu(x) = \nabla^2 (1) = \mathbf 0,
$$
where the second-derivative interchange is licensed by (R3). Therefore
$\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[\nabla^2 \ell(\boldsymbol\theta; X)] = \mathbf 0 - \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[\mathbf s \mathbf s^\top] = -\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)$,
which rearranges to @eq-info-equality. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters.** The information equality is a duality: *how variable the slope of the log-likelihood
is across samples* (the score variance, left side) equals *how curved the log-likelihood is on average*
(minus the expected Hessian, right side). This is the hinge of the whole chapter. It is why the same
matrix $\mathcal I$ appears both as the variance in the central limit theorem for the score and as the
curvature that converts that noise into estimator noise; it makes the MLE's variance equal to
$\mathcal I^{-1}$ (@thm-mle-asymptotic-normality), it powers the Cramér-Rao bound, and its *failure* under
misspecification is exactly what forces the sandwich variance of @sec-m-estimation. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The information in independent data adds. This additivity is why precision scales linearly with sample
size, and it is the reason the per-observation information $\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)$ is the natural
unit.

::: {#cor-information-additivity}
## Additivity of information
For iid data the sample score $\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \sum_i \mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X_i)$
has mean zero and
$$
\mathcal I_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}\bigl(\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta)\bigr)
= n\,\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta).
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
By @lem-score-mean-zero each summand has mean zero, so $\mathbb E[\mathbf s_n] = \mathbf 0$. The summands
are iid, hence uncorrelated, so the covariance of the sum is the sum of the covariances:
$\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf s_n) = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X_i)) = n\,\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)$
by @def-fisher-information. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
## Per-observation information versus sample information (a common source of confusion)
Two informations are now in play, and standard errors depend on getting the factor of $n$ right. Keep
them straight with this table.

| Symbol | Name | Formula | Refers to |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)$ | per-observation information | $\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X))$ | a single observation |
| $\mathcal I_n(\boldsymbol\theta)$ | sample information | $n\,\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)$ | the whole sample of size $n$ |

The variance of the MLE is governed by the *sample* information: in large samples
$\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) \approx \mathcal I_n(\boldsymbol\theta)^{-1} = \tfrac1n\,\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)^{-1}$,
and the standard error is the square root of a diagonal entry. The per-observation $\mathcal I$ is the
fixed "information rate"; multiplying by $n$ and inverting is what makes the standard error shrink like
$1/\sqrt n$. For the running example, $\mathcal I(p) = 1/[p(1 - p)]$, the sample information is
$\mathcal I_n(p) = n/[p(1 - p)]$, and $\mathrm{Var}(\hat p) \approx p(1 - p)/n$. At $\hat p = 0.4$,
$n = 25$: $\mathcal I_n(\hat p) = 25/0.24 = 104.17$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat p) = 0.24/25 = 0.0096$.
A recurring novice slip is to invert $\mathcal I$ instead of $\mathcal I_n$, which inflates the standard
error by a factor of $\sqrt n$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Maximum likelihood and its invariance {#sec-mle}

::: {#def-mle}
## Maximum likelihood estimator
A *maximum likelihood estimator* (MLE) is any parameter value maximizing the likelihood, equivalently
the log-likelihood,
$$
\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}} = \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n
\in \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\boldsymbol\theta \in \Theta} L_n(\boldsymbol\theta)
= \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\boldsymbol\theta \in \Theta} \ell_n(\boldsymbol\theta).
$$
When $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$ lies in the interior of $\Theta$ and $\ell_n$ is differentiable there,
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$ solves the *likelihood (score) equations*
$\mathbf s_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) = \mathbf 0$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** The MLE is the parameter value under which the data we actually saw would have
been *most probable*: the top of the log-likelihood hill, where the score (slope) is zero. For the
running example this is just $\hat p = \bar X_n = 0.40$, the sample proportion. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

Maximization is invariant under reparameterization, which is one of the most useful practical properties
of the MLE: to estimate any function of the parameter by maximum likelihood, just plug in.

::: {#prp-mle-invariance}
## Invariance of the MLE
Let $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$ be an MLE of $\boldsymbol\theta$.

(i) If $h : \Theta \to \mathrm H$ is a bijection and the model is reparameterized by
$\boldsymbol\eta = h(\boldsymbol\theta)$, then $h(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)$ is an MLE of
$\boldsymbol\eta$.

(ii) For an arbitrary (not necessarily injective) function $h : \Theta \to \mathrm H$, define the
*induced (profile) likelihood* $L_n^{*}(\boldsymbol\eta) = \sup\{L_n(\boldsymbol\theta) : h(\boldsymbol\theta) = \boldsymbol\eta\}$.
Then $h(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)$ maximizes $L_n^{*}$; we call $h(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)$ the MLE of
$\boldsymbol\eta = h(\boldsymbol\theta)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
*(i)* Write the likelihood in the new parameterization as
$\tilde L_n(\boldsymbol\eta) = L_n(h^{-1}(\boldsymbol\eta))$. Since $h^{-1}$ is a bijection of
$\mathrm H$ onto $\Theta$, ranging $\boldsymbol\eta$ over $\mathrm H$ ranges
$h^{-1}(\boldsymbol\eta)$ over all of $\Theta$, so
$\sup_{\boldsymbol\eta} \tilde L_n(\boldsymbol\eta) = \sup_{\boldsymbol\theta} L_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = L_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)$,
and the supremum is attained at $\boldsymbol\eta = h(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)$ because
$\tilde L_n(h(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)) = L_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)$.

*(ii)* By construction $L_n^{*}(\boldsymbol\eta) \le \sup_{\boldsymbol\theta} L_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = L_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)$
for every $\boldsymbol\eta$, since each $L_n^{*}(\boldsymbol\eta)$ is a supremum over a subset of
$\Theta$. Evaluating at $\boldsymbol\eta^{*} = h(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)$, the defining set
$\{\boldsymbol\theta : h(\boldsymbol\theta) = \boldsymbol\eta^{*}\}$ contains $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$,
so $L_n^{*}(\boldsymbol\eta^{*}) \ge L_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)$. The two inequalities force
$L_n^{*}(\boldsymbol\eta^{*}) = L_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) = \max_{\boldsymbol\eta} L_n^{*}(\boldsymbol\eta)$,
so $\boldsymbol\eta^{*} = h(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)$ maximizes $L_n^{*}$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters, and what "profile" means.** Part (i) is the workhorse behind every transformed
estimate in the book: to get the MLE of an odds ratio, a risk ratio, a hazard ratio, or a marginal
effect, you fit the model once and *plug the MLE into the transformation*; no separate maximization is
needed. Part (ii) handles the case where the transformation $h$ throws away some parameters (nuisance
parameters). The *profile likelihood* $L_n^{*}(\boldsymbol\eta)$ is built by maximizing out everything
except the target $\boldsymbol\eta$, tracing a one-dimensional ridge ("profile") across the full
likelihood surface; it is the object inverted to get the profile-likelihood confidence intervals of
@sec-tests, which is why we record it now even though we do not use it until then. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Consistency of the MLE {#sec-consistency}

**Why prove this?** As a practitioner you may take for granted that more data means a better estimate.
Consistency is the theorem that makes that faith legitimate: it is the guarantee that, as trials grow, the
MLE, and with it the network meta-analysis and MAIC estimates of later chapters, stops being
systematically wrong and settles on the true value. Without it, none of the asymptotic standard errors
below would describe anything real.

We now prove that the MLE converges to the truth. The argument has three clean pieces: a population
criterion uniquely maximized at $\boldsymbol\theta_0$ (the information inequality), a uniform law of large
numbers transferring the sample criterion to the population one, and an argmax-continuity lemma. The
first piece relies on Jensen's inequality (@thm-jensen).

::: {#lem-kl-information-inequality}
## Information inequality
Let $\boldsymbol\theta_0$ be the true parameter and suppose the model is identifiable
(@def-statistical-model). For every $\boldsymbol\theta \in \Theta$ with
$\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}\bigl|\log f(X;\boldsymbol\theta)\bigr| < \infty$,
$$
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}\!\bigl[\log f(X;\boldsymbol\theta_0)\bigr]
\;\ge\;
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}\!\bigl[\log f(X;\boldsymbol\theta)\bigr],
$$
with equality if and only if $\boldsymbol\theta = \boldsymbol\theta_0$. Equivalently, the
Kullback-Leibler divergence
$\mathrm{KL}(f_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}\,\|\,f_{\boldsymbol\theta}) = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}[\log(f(X;\boldsymbol\theta_0)/f(X;\boldsymbol\theta))]$
is nonnegative and vanishes only at $\boldsymbol\theta_0$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Consider the ratio $r(X) = f(X;\boldsymbol\theta) / f(X;\boldsymbol\theta_0)$, defined where
$f(X;\boldsymbol\theta_0) > 0$. The function $\varphi(u) = -\log u$ is strictly convex on $(0,\infty)$.
By Jensen's inequality (@thm-jensen),
$$
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}\!\bigl[-\log r(X)\bigr]
\;\ge\; -\log \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}[r(X)].
$$
The right-hand expectation is
$$
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}[r(X)]
= \int_{\{f_{\boldsymbol\theta_0} > 0\}} \frac{f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)}{f(x;\boldsymbol\theta_0)}\, f(x;\boldsymbol\theta_0)\, d\nu(x)
= \int_{\{f_{\boldsymbol\theta_0} > 0\}} f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\, d\nu(x) \le 1,
$$
so $-\log \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}[r(X)] \ge 0$. Therefore
$\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}[-\log r(X)] = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}[\log f(X;\boldsymbol\theta_0)] - \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}[\log f(X;\boldsymbol\theta)] \ge 0$,
which is the claimed inequality and shows $\mathrm{KL} \ge 0$.

For equality: strict convexity of $\varphi$ makes Jensen an equality only if $r(X)$ is
$P_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}$-almost surely constant, say $r(X) = c$. Then
$f(X;\boldsymbol\theta) = c\, f(X;\boldsymbol\theta_0)$ a.s., and integrating both sides forces $c = 1$
(both are densities), so $f(\cdot;\boldsymbol\theta) = f(\cdot;\boldsymbol\theta_0)$ $\nu$-almost
everywhere. By identifiability this means $\boldsymbol\theta = \boldsymbol\theta_0$. Conversely
$\boldsymbol\theta = \boldsymbol\theta_0$ gives equality trivially. $\square$
:::

The population criterion is $M(\boldsymbol\theta) = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}[\log f(X;\boldsymbol\theta)]$
and the sample criterion is $M_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \tfrac1n \ell_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \tfrac1n \sum_i \log f(X_i;\boldsymbol\theta)$.
For each fixed $\boldsymbol\theta$ the WLLN gives $M_n(\boldsymbol\theta) \xrightarrow{p} M(\boldsymbol\theta)$;
to control the maximizer we need this uniformly in $\boldsymbol\theta$. We state the uniform law as a
cited prerequisite.

::: {#lem-uniform-lln}
## Uniform law of large numbers
Let $\Theta$ be compact, let $\boldsymbol\theta \mapsto \log f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)$ be continuous for
$\nu$-almost every $x$, and suppose the *envelope condition*
$\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}\bigl[\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta \in \Theta} |\log f(X;\boldsymbol\theta)|\bigr] < \infty$
holds. Then $M$ is continuous on $\Theta$ and
$$
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta \in \Theta} \bigl|M_n(\boldsymbol\theta) - M(\boldsymbol\theta)\bigr|
\xrightarrow{p} 0 .
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
This is a standard consequence of compactness, almost-everywhere continuity, and the integrable envelope;
the proof covers $\Theta$ by finitely many small balls, applies the pointwise WLLN at the centers, and
controls the oscillation inside each ball with the envelope and dominated convergence. See
@bingham2010regression and a standard text on asymptotic statistics; we take it as given. $\square$
:::

::: {#lem-argmax-consistency}
## Argmax consistency
Let $M : \Theta \to \mathbb R$ be continuous on a compact set $\Theta$ with a unique maximizer
$\boldsymbol\theta_0$. Let $M_n$ be random functions with
$\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta} |M_n(\boldsymbol\theta) - M(\boldsymbol\theta)| \xrightarrow{p} 0$, and let
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \in \arg\max_{\boldsymbol\theta} M_n(\boldsymbol\theta)$. Then
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta_0$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Fix $\varepsilon > 0$ and let $B_\varepsilon = \{\boldsymbol\theta \in \Theta : \|\boldsymbol\theta - \boldsymbol\theta_0\| \ge \varepsilon\}$.
This set is closed, hence compact, so the continuous $M$ attains its maximum over $B_\varepsilon$ at some
point; because $\boldsymbol\theta_0 \notin B_\varepsilon$ and $\boldsymbol\theta_0$ is the *unique*
maximizer of $M$, this maximum is strictly below $M(\boldsymbol\theta_0)$. Set
$$
\delta = M(\boldsymbol\theta_0) - \sup_{\boldsymbol\theta \in B_\varepsilon} M(\boldsymbol\theta) > 0 .
$$
Let $U_n = \sup_{\boldsymbol\theta} |M_n(\boldsymbol\theta) - M(\boldsymbol\theta)|$ and work on the event
$\{U_n < \delta/2\}$. On this event, for any $\boldsymbol\theta \in B_\varepsilon$,
$$
M_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) \ge M_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0) > M(\boldsymbol\theta_0) - \tfrac{\delta}{2}
= \sup_{B_\varepsilon} M + \tfrac{\delta}{2} \ge M(\boldsymbol\theta) + \tfrac{\delta}{2} > M_n(\boldsymbol\theta),
$$
using, in order, that $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$ maximizes $M_n$, the bound $U_n < \delta/2$ at
$\boldsymbol\theta_0$, the definition of $\delta$, and again $U_n < \delta/2$ at $\boldsymbol\theta$.
Thus no point of $B_\varepsilon$ can be the maximizer of $M_n$, so
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \notin B_\varepsilon$, that is
$\|\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0\| < \varepsilon$. Hence
$$
P\bigl(\|\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0\| \ge \varepsilon\bigr)
\le P\bigl(U_n \ge \tfrac{\delta}{2}\bigr) \to 0 ,
$$
by the uniform convergence hypothesis. As $\varepsilon$ was arbitrary,
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta_0$. $\square$
:::

::: {#thm-mle-consistency}
## Consistency of the MLE
Suppose $X_1, \dots, X_n$ are iid from $f(\cdot;\boldsymbol\theta_0)$ and:

(C1) $\Theta \subseteq \mathbb R^p$ is compact and $\boldsymbol\theta_0 \in \Theta$;

(C2) the model is identifiable (@def-statistical-model);

(C3) $\boldsymbol\theta \mapsto \log f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)$ is continuous for $\nu$-almost every $x$;

(C4) the envelope condition
$\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}\bigl[\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}|\log f(X;\boldsymbol\theta)|\bigr] < \infty$
holds.

Then any MLE sequence $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$ satisfies
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta_0$.
:::

::: {.proof}
The MLE maximizes $M_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \tfrac1n \ell_n(\boldsymbol\theta)$ (dividing the
log-likelihood by $n$ does not move the argmax). By @lem-kl-information-inequality and identifiability
(C2), the population criterion
$M(\boldsymbol\theta) = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}[\log f(X;\boldsymbol\theta)]$ has a *unique*
maximizer at $\boldsymbol\theta_0$; the envelope (C4) makes $M$ finite, and with (C3) it is continuous by
@lem-uniform-lln, which simultaneously gives the uniform convergence
$\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta}|M_n(\boldsymbol\theta) - M(\boldsymbol\theta)| \xrightarrow{p} 0$. Compactness
(C1), continuity, the unique maximum, and uniform convergence are exactly the hypotheses of
@lem-argmax-consistency, which yields $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta_0$.
$\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters, with the running example.** For the Bernoulli the hypotheses are easy to check:
$\Theta = [0, 1]$ is compact (C1), the model is identifiable since different $p$ give different
distributions (C2), $\log f(x; p)$ is continuous in $p$ (C3), and the envelope holds, so the theorem gives
$\hat p_n \xrightarrow{p} p_0$. In words, the trial's response rate converges to the true response rate.
Translated to the book's subject, this is what guarantees that, with enough patients, an indirect
comparison built from such estimates converges to the true contrast rather than to a biased value.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
Compactness of $\Theta$ (C1) is the only restrictive condition, and it can be relaxed. The standard
device is to show the log-likelihood is eventually larger at $\boldsymbol\theta_0$ than outside a compact
set (so the maximizer cannot escape to the boundary), then apply the theorem on the compact core.
Alternatively, the *Cramér* approach abandons the global maximizer and proves that the score equation
$\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \mathbf 0$ has, with probability tending to one, a root within
$O_p(n^{-1/2})$ of $\boldsymbol\theta_0$; that local root is consistent and asymptotically normal even
when the global MLE is ill-behaved. We use the global form here for definiteness.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Asymptotic normality of the MLE {#sec-asymptotic-normality}

Consistency says the MLE lands near $\boldsymbol\theta_0$. Asymptotic normality describes the
*distribution* of the residual error $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0$, rescaled by
$\sqrt n$. The proof is the canonical "Taylor-expand the score" argument: the score vanishes at the MLE,
expand it about the truth, and read off a ratio of a central-limit term over an information term.

::: {#thm-mle-asymptotic-normality}
## Asymptotic normality of the MLE
Suppose $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta_0$ (for instance by
@thm-mle-consistency), and in addition:

(A1) $\boldsymbol\theta_0 \in \mathrm{int}\,\Theta$ and the model is regular (@def-regular-model) on a
neighborhood of $\boldsymbol\theta_0$, so $\ell(\boldsymbol\theta; x)$ is twice continuously
differentiable there;

(A2) the Fisher information $\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)$ is finite and positive definite;

(A3) the Hessian satisfies a local uniform law of large numbers: there is a neighborhood
$\mathcal U$ of $\boldsymbol\theta_0$ with
$\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}\bigl[\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\mathcal U}\|\nabla^2\ell(\boldsymbol\theta;X)\|\bigr] < \infty$,
so that $\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\mathcal U}\|\tfrac1n\sum_i \nabla^2\ell(\boldsymbol\theta;X_i) - \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}[\nabla^2\ell(\boldsymbol\theta;X)]\| \xrightarrow{p} 0$.

Then, with probability tending to one $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$ solves
$\mathbf s_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) = \mathbf 0$, and
$$
\sqrt n\,\bigl(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0\bigr)
\xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N_p\!\bigl(\mathbf 0,\; \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}\bigr).
$$ {#eq-mle-asymptotic-normality}
:::

::: {.proof}
**Step 1 (the estimator solves the score equation).** Since
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta_0$ and $\boldsymbol\theta_0$ is interior
(A1), with probability tending to one $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$ lies in the open neighborhood
$\mathcal U$ where $\ell_n$ is differentiable and is an interior maximizer, so the first-order condition
$\mathbf s_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) = \nabla\ell_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) = \mathbf 0$ holds. We
work on this event henceforth.

**Step 2 (exact first-order expansion with integral remainder).** Apply the fundamental theorem of
calculus to the gradient field $\boldsymbol\theta \mapsto \mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta)$ along the
segment from $\boldsymbol\theta_0$ to $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$, both eventually in $\mathcal U$. (This
is the fundamental theorem of calculus applied to each component of the vector field $\mathbf s_n$ along
the path; the bracketed matrix $\bar{\mathbf H}_n$ is the Hessian averaged over the segment, playing the
role of the mean-value remainder familiar from the scalar Taylor expansion.) With
$\mathbf H_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \nabla^2 \ell_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \nabla \mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta)$,
$$
\mathbf 0 = \mathbf s_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)
= \mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0) + \underbrace{\left[\int_0^1 \mathbf H_n\bigl(\boldsymbol\theta_0 + t(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)\bigr)\, dt\right]}_{=:\; \bar{\mathbf H}_n}\,(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0).
$$
Define $\mathbf A_n = -\tfrac1n \bar{\mathbf H}_n$. Then, multiplying by $-1/n$ and rearranging,
$$
\mathbf A_n\,\sqrt n\,(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)
= \tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}\,\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0).
$$ {#eq-an-system}

**Step 3 (the score term is asymptotically normal).** Write
$\tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0) = \sqrt n\,\bigl(\tfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta_0; X_i) - \mathbf 0\bigr)$.
The per-observation scores $\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta_0; X_i)$ are iid with mean
$\mathbf 0$ (@lem-score-mean-zero) and covariance $\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)$
(@def-fisher-information), finite by (A2). The multivariate CLT gives
$$
\tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}\,\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0) \xrightarrow{d} \mathbf Z, \qquad \mathbf Z \sim \mathcal N_p\bigl(\mathbf 0,\, \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)\bigr).
$$ {#eq-score-clt}

**Step 4 (the averaged Hessian converges to the information).** Each intermediate point
$\boldsymbol\theta_0 + t(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)$ lies between $\boldsymbol\theta_0$
and $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$, hence converges in probability to $\boldsymbol\theta_0$ uniformly in
$t \in [0,1]$. By the local uniform law (A3), the map
$\boldsymbol\theta \mapsto -\tfrac1n\sum_i \nabla^2\ell(\boldsymbol\theta; X_i)$ converges in probability,
uniformly over $\mathcal U$, to the continuous limit
$\boldsymbol\theta \mapsto -\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_0}[\nabla^2\ell(\boldsymbol\theta; X)]$, which at
$\boldsymbol\theta = \boldsymbol\theta_0$ equals $\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)$ by the information
equality (@thm-information-equality). Combining uniform convergence with
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p}\boldsymbol\theta_0$ and continuity of the limit,
$$
\mathbf A_n = -\tfrac1n \int_0^1 \mathbf H_n\bigl(\boldsymbol\theta_0 + t(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)\bigr)\, dt
\xrightarrow{p} \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0).
$$ {#eq-an-converges}

**Step 5 (solve and apply Slutsky).** By (A2) the limit $\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)$ is invertible.
Matrix inversion is continuous at any nonsingular matrix, so the continuous mapping theorem
(@thm-continuous-mapping) gives $\mathbf A_n^{-1} \xrightarrow{p} \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}$
(in particular $\mathbf A_n$ is invertible with probability tending to one). Solving @eq-an-system and
applying Slutsky (@thm-slutsky) to the product of the convergent-in-probability matrix
$\mathbf A_n^{-1}$ and the convergent-in-distribution vector @eq-score-clt,
$$
\sqrt n\,(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)
= \mathbf A_n^{-1}\, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0)
\xrightarrow{d} \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}\,\mathbf Z .
$$
Finally, the affine (here linear) image of a Gaussian is Gaussian (@thm-mvn-linear): with
$\mathbf B = \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}$ and $\mathbf Z \sim \mathcal N_p(\mathbf 0, \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0))$,
$$
\mathbf B\mathbf Z \sim \mathcal N_p\bigl(\mathbf 0,\; \mathbf B\,\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)\,\mathbf B^\top\bigr)
= \mathcal N_p\bigl(\mathbf 0,\; \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}\,\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)\,\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}\bigr)
= \mathcal N_p\bigl(\mathbf 0,\; \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}\bigr),
$$
using the symmetry of $\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}$. This is @eq-mle-asymptotic-normality.
$\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters.** This theorem is the source of the ubiquitous "estimate $\pm 1.96$ standard errors"
interval. It says the MLE is approximately
$\mathcal N_p(\boldsymbol\theta_0,\, \tfrac1n\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1})$ in large samples, so
every Wald confidence interval and $z$-test in a regression printout is an application of
@eq-mle-asymptotic-normality. The idea behind the proof, stripped of detail: at the maximum the slope
(score) is zero; near the truth the slope is approximately linear, with slope equal to the curvature
(information); solving that linear relation turns the central-limit noise in the score into Gaussian noise
in the estimator, scaled by the inverse information. For the running example,
$\sqrt n(\hat p - p) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N(0,\, p(1 - p))$ because $\mathcal I(p)^{-1} = p(1 - p)$.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
## Estimating the asymptotic variance
@eq-mle-asymptotic-normality says $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$ is approximately
$\mathcal N_p(\boldsymbol\theta_0,\, \tfrac1n \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1})$ in large samples, so a
standard error for the $b$-th coordinate is the square root of the $(b,b)$ entry of
$\tfrac1n \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}$. In practice $\boldsymbol\theta_0$ is unknown, so one of two
consistent plug-ins is used: the *expected information* evaluated at the estimate,
$\mathcal I(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)$, or the *observed information*
$\mathbf J_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) = -\nabla^2 \ell_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)$, which by Step 4
satisfies $\tfrac1n \mathbf J_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) \xrightarrow{p} \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)$.
Either yields a valid asymptotic variance estimate by Slutsky; the observed information requires no
expectation and is what most software reports. The two agree in large samples; they can differ in small
samples or under departures from the model, where the observed form uses the *actual* curvature at your
estimate while the expected form averages curvature over hypothetical datasets. Concretely, what software
prints as a "standard error" is the square root of a diagonal entry of the inverted observed information
$\mathbf J_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)^{-1}$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## The Cramér-Rao lower bound and efficiency {#sec-cramer-rao}

**Why a lower bound matters for indirect comparisons.** Every method in this book reports a standard
error, and a natural question is whether it could have done better with the same data. The Cramér-Rao
bound is the yardstick: it is the smallest variance any unbiased estimator can achieve under a correctly
specified regular model, so when MAIC or a network meta-analysis reports a precision you can ask whether
it is near this optimum or is leaving information on the table. It is a theoretical benchmark, not
something you compute on each dataset, but it explains *why* the inverse Fisher information is the natural
ideal variance.

How small can the variance of an unbiased estimator be? The Cramér-Rao bound answers: no smaller than the
inverse Fisher information. The proof is a single application of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality
(@thm-cauchy-schwarz-ip), using that the score has mean zero.

::: {#thm-cramer-rao}
## Cramér-Rao lower bound
Let the model be regular (@def-regular-model) at $\boldsymbol\theta$, and let $T = T(X)$ be a
statistic with $\mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T) < \infty$ whose mean
$g(\boldsymbol\theta) = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[T]$ is differentiable with the differentiation
passing under the integral sign.

(i) **Scalar parameter** ($p = 1$). Then
$$
\mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T) \;\ge\; \frac{g'(\boldsymbol\theta)^2}{\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)} .
$$ {#eq-crlb-scalar}
In particular, if $T$ is unbiased for $\boldsymbol\theta$ (so $g(\boldsymbol\theta) = \boldsymbol\theta$,
$g' = 1$), then $\mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T) \ge 1/\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)$. Equality holds
if and only if $T - g(\boldsymbol\theta)$ is, almost surely, a (deterministic) multiple of the score
$\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X)$.

(ii) **Vector parameter.** If $\mathbf T$ is an unbiased estimator of $\boldsymbol\theta \in \mathbb R^p$,
then in the Loewner (positive-semidefinite) order
$$
\mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf T) \;\succeq\; \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)^{-1} ,
$$ {#eq-crlb-matrix}
that is, $\mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf T) - \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)^{-1}$ is positive
semidefinite. Here $A \succeq B$ (the *Loewner order*) means $A - B$ is positive semidefinite; concretely
it says every scalar combination $\mathbf v^\top\mathbf T$ has variance at least
$\mathbf v^\top\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)^{-1}\mathbf v$, so the estimator beats the bound in no
direction.
:::

::: {.proof}
*(i)* Differentiate the identity $g(\boldsymbol\theta) = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[T] = \int T(x)\, f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\, d\nu(x)$
under the integral sign:
$$
g'(\boldsymbol\theta) = \int T(x)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial\boldsymbol\theta} f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\, d\nu(x)
= \int T(x)\, \mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; x)\, f(x;\boldsymbol\theta)\, d\nu(x)
= \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}\bigl[T\,\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X)\bigr],
$$
using $\partial_{\boldsymbol\theta} f = \mathbf s\, f$. Because the score has mean zero
(@lem-score-mean-zero), $\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[T\,\mathbf s] = \mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T, \mathbf s)$,
so $g'(\boldsymbol\theta) = \mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T, \mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X))$. The space
of mean-zero square-integrable random variables under $P_{\boldsymbol\theta}$ is an inner product space
with $\langle U, V\rangle = \mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(U, V)$; applying the Cauchy-Schwarz
inequality (@thm-cauchy-schwarz-ip) to $T - g(\boldsymbol\theta)$ and the score,
$$
g'(\boldsymbol\theta)^2 = \mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T, \mathbf s)^2
\le \mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T)\,\mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf s)
= \mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(T)\, \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta) .
$$
Dividing by $\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta) > 0$ gives @eq-crlb-scalar. Cauchy-Schwarz is an equality
exactly when the two vectors are linearly dependent, that is when $T - g(\boldsymbol\theta) = a(\boldsymbol\theta)\,\mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X)$
almost surely for some constant $a(\boldsymbol\theta)$.

*(ii)* Let $\mathbf s = \mathbf s(\boldsymbol\theta; X)$ and center $\mathbf U = \mathbf T - \boldsymbol\theta$
(mean zero by unbiasedness). The componentwise version of the scalar computation gives, for each pair
$(a, b)$, $\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[U_a\, s_b] = \partial_{\theta_b}\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[T_a] = \partial_{\theta_b}\theta_a = \mathbb 1\{a = b\}$,
so the cross-covariance is the identity:
$\mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf T, \mathbf s) = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[\mathbf U \mathbf s^\top] = I_p$.
Stack $\mathbf U$ and $\mathbf s$ into a $2p$-vector; its covariance matrix is positive semidefinite
(@thm-cov-psd):
$$
\mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}\!\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf U \\ \mathbf s\end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} \mathrm{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf T) & I_p \\[2pt] I_p & \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta) \end{pmatrix}
=: \begin{pmatrix} \Sigma_T & I_p \\ I_p & \mathcal I \end{pmatrix} \succeq 0 .
$$
Since $\mathcal I \succ 0$, evaluate the quadratic form of this block matrix on the cleverly chosen vector
$(\,\mathbf v^\top,\; -(\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf v)^\top)^\top$ for arbitrary $\mathbf v \in \mathbb R^p$.
The second block $-\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf v$ is engineered so that the identity cross-blocks cancel,
leaving only the difference $\Sigma_T - \mathcal I^{-1}$; this cancellation is the algebraic content of
the *Schur complement* of the $\mathcal I$ block:
$$
0 \le \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf v \\ -\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf v\end{pmatrix}^{\!\top}\!
\begin{pmatrix} \Sigma_T & I_p \\ I_p & \mathcal I \end{pmatrix}\!
\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf v \\ -\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf v\end{pmatrix}
= \mathbf v^\top \Sigma_T \mathbf v - 2\,\mathbf v^\top \mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf v + \mathbf v^\top \mathcal I^{-1}\mathcal I\,\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf v
= \mathbf v^\top\bigl(\Sigma_T - \mathcal I^{-1}\bigr)\mathbf v .
$$
As $\mathbf v$ was arbitrary, $\Sigma_T - \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)^{-1} \succeq 0$, which is
@eq-crlb-matrix. (This is precisely the Schur-complement positivity of the block matrix.) $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters.** Read the scalar bound @eq-crlb-scalar as: precision is capped by information. You
cannot make an unbiased estimator arbitrarily precise; the best achievable variance is
$1/\mathcal I_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = 1/[n\,\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)]$, which is why "more information"
and "more data" both mean "smaller standard error." When a later method attains this bound (the MLE does,
asymptotically), you know no regular competitor can do better with the same model and data.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The bound motivates a precise notion of "best possible" estimator.

::: {#def-efficient-estimator}
## Efficiency and asymptotic efficiency
An unbiased estimator $T$ of a scalar $g(\boldsymbol\theta)$ is *(Cramér-Rao) efficient* if it attains the
bound @eq-crlb-scalar with equality for all $\boldsymbol\theta$. A consistent estimator sequence
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$ with
$\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N_p(\mathbf 0, \mathbf V(\boldsymbol\theta_0))$
is *asymptotically efficient* if $\mathbf V(\boldsymbol\theta_0) = \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}$,
the smallest asymptotic covariance permitted (in the Loewner order) for regular estimators. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#cor-mle-efficient}
## The MLE is asymptotically efficient
Under the hypotheses of @thm-mle-asymptotic-normality, the MLE is asymptotically efficient: its
asymptotic covariance $\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}$ equals the per-observation Cramér-Rao bound.
:::

::: {.proof}
Immediate by comparing @eq-mle-asymptotic-normality with @def-efficient-estimator: the asymptotic
covariance of $\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)$ is $\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}$.
$\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters.** Asymptotic efficiency is the precise sense in which maximum likelihood is "as good
as it gets": no regular estimator can have a smaller asymptotic variance than the MLE's
$\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}$. The practical payoff is reassurance: when a systematic review uses
likelihood-based methods (most network meta-analyses, and ML-NMR), it is not leaving precision on the
table relative to any competing regular estimator built from the same model. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
The matrix bound @eq-crlb-matrix is a *finite-sample* statement about unbiased estimators, while
