@def-efficient-estimator's asymptotic optimality is a statement about the limiting distribution of
possibly biased estimators. The rigorous bridge that no regular estimator can have asymptotic covariance
below $\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}$ is the Hájek-Le Cam convolution theorem and the local
asymptotic minimax theorem; we cite these (see @bingham2010regression and the asymptotic-statistics
literature) rather than prove them, as they require the local asymptotic normality framework beyond this
chapter. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## M-estimation and the sandwich variance {#sec-m-estimation}

Maximum likelihood is the special case, with $\boldsymbol\psi$ equal to the score, of a far more general
construction: define an estimator as the solution of an *estimating equation*. This generality is exactly
what later chapters need. A MAIC estimator (Chapter 18) solves a weighting equation that is not the score
of any correctly specified likelihood, yet it is asymptotically normal, and its correct standard error is
the *sandwich* variance defined below.

::: {#def-m-estimator}
## M-estimator and estimating equation
Let $\boldsymbol\psi(x; \boldsymbol\theta) \in \mathbb R^p$ be a known *estimating function*. An
*M-estimator* $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$ is a solution of the estimating equation
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \boldsymbol\psi(X_i; \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) = \mathbf 0 .
$$ {#eq-estimating-equation}
The *target* (or estimand) is the value $\boldsymbol\theta^{*}$ solving the population equation
$\mathbb E_{P}[\boldsymbol\psi(X; \boldsymbol\theta^{*})] = \mathbf 0$, where $P$ is the *true*
data-generating distribution, which need not belong to the working model. The MLE is the M-estimator with
$\boldsymbol\psi = \mathbf s$, the score, in which case $\boldsymbol\theta^{*} = \boldsymbol\theta_0$ under
correct specification. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** An M-estimator is defined not by maximizing something but by *solving an equation*
$\sum_i \boldsymbol\psi(X_i; \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) = \mathbf 0$. Choosing $\boldsymbol\psi$ to be the
score recovers maximum likelihood, but $\boldsymbol\psi$ can be any sensible estimating function, even one
with no likelihood behind it. The crucial shift is the *target* $\boldsymbol\theta^{*}$: it is whatever
value the equation aims at in the real world $P$, which need not be the "true parameter" of any correct
model. This is the honest setting for MAIC, whose weighting equation is a computational device, not a
believed model. A one-covariate MAIC balancing equation has the schematic form
$\sum_i w_i(\boldsymbol\theta)\,(x_i - \bar x^{*}) = 0$, "choose weights so the weighted covariate mean
equals the target population mean $\bar x^{*}$"; Chapter 18 makes this precise. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The asymptotic distribution of an M-estimator follows the same Taylor expansion as the MLE, but the
variance no longer collapses to a single information matrix; it is a sandwich of two matrices.

::: {#thm-m-estimator-normal}
## Asymptotic normality of M-estimators
Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be iid from $P$, let $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$ solve @eq-estimating-equation, and
suppose $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta^{*}$, where
$\mathbb E_P[\boldsymbol\psi(X; \boldsymbol\theta^{*})] = \mathbf 0$. Assume $\boldsymbol\psi(x; \cdot)$ is
continuously differentiable near $\boldsymbol\theta^{*}$, the matrix
$$
\mathbf A(\boldsymbol\theta^{*}) = -\,\mathbb E_P\!\bigl[\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\boldsymbol\psi(X; \boldsymbol\theta^{*})\bigr]
\quad(\text{the ``bread''})
$$
is nonsingular, the matrix
$\mathbf B(\boldsymbol\theta^{*}) = \mathbb E_P\!\bigl[\boldsymbol\psi(X; \boldsymbol\theta^{*})\,\boldsymbol\psi(X; \boldsymbol\theta^{*})^\top\bigr]$
(the ``meat'') is finite, and $\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\boldsymbol\psi$ obeys a local uniform law of
large numbers near $\boldsymbol\theta^{*}$: there is a neighborhood $\mathcal U^{*}$ of
$\boldsymbol\theta^{*}$ with
$\mathbb E_P\bigl[\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\mathcal U^{*}}\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\boldsymbol\psi(X;\boldsymbol\theta)\|\bigr] < \infty$
and
$\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\mathcal U^{*}}\bigl\|\tfrac1n\sum_i \nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\boldsymbol\psi(X_i;\boldsymbol\theta) - \mathbb E_P[\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\boldsymbol\psi(X;\boldsymbol\theta)]\bigr\| \xrightarrow{p} 0$,
exactly parallel to (A3) of @thm-mle-asymptotic-normality. Then
$$
\sqrt n\,\bigl(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta^{*}\bigr)
\xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N_p\!\Bigl(\mathbf 0,\; \mathbf A(\boldsymbol\theta^{*})^{-1}\,\mathbf B(\boldsymbol\theta^{*})\,\mathbf A(\boldsymbol\theta^{*})^{-\top}\Bigr) ,
$$ {#eq-sandwich-asymptotic}
where $\mathbf A^{-\top}$ abbreviates $(\mathbf A^{-1})^\top = (\mathbf A^\top)^{-1}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $\boldsymbol\Psi_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \boldsymbol\psi(X_i; \boldsymbol\theta)$, so
$\boldsymbol\Psi_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) = \mathbf 0$. As in Step 2 of
@thm-mle-asymptotic-normality, the fundamental theorem of calculus along the segment from
$\boldsymbol\theta^{*}$ to $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$ gives
$$
\mathbf 0 = \boldsymbol\Psi_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)
= \boldsymbol\Psi_n(\boldsymbol\theta^{*}) + \Bigl[\textstyle\int_0^1 \nabla\boldsymbol\Psi_n\bigl(\boldsymbol\theta^{*} + t(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta^{*})\bigr)\, dt\Bigr](\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta^{*}),
$$
hence with $\mathbf A_n = -\tfrac1n\int_0^1 \nabla\boldsymbol\Psi_n(\boldsymbol\theta^{*} + t(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta^{*}))\,dt$,
$$
\mathbf A_n\,\sqrt n\,(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta^{*}) = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}\,\boldsymbol\Psi_n(\boldsymbol\theta^{*}).
$$
The summands $\boldsymbol\psi(X_i; \boldsymbol\theta^{*})$ are iid with mean $\mathbf 0$ (by the definition
of $\boldsymbol\theta^{*}$) and covariance $\mathbf B(\boldsymbol\theta^{*})$, so the multivariate CLT
gives $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}\boldsymbol\Psi_n(\boldsymbol\theta^{*}) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N_p(\mathbf 0, \mathbf B(\boldsymbol\theta^{*}))$.
By consistency, the local uniform law, and continuity (exactly as in Step 4 of
@thm-mle-asymptotic-normality), $\mathbf A_n \xrightarrow{p} \mathbf A(\boldsymbol\theta^{*})$, which is
nonsingular, so $\mathbf A_n^{-1} \xrightarrow{p} \mathbf A(\boldsymbol\theta^{*})^{-1}$ by continuous
mapping (@thm-continuous-mapping). Slutsky (@thm-slutsky) and @thm-mvn-linear give
$$
\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta^{*}) = \mathbf A_n^{-1}\,\tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}\boldsymbol\Psi_n(\boldsymbol\theta^{*})
\xrightarrow{d} \mathbf A^{-1}\mathcal N_p(\mathbf 0, \mathbf B)
= \mathcal N_p\bigl(\mathbf 0, \mathbf A^{-1}\mathbf B\,\mathbf A^{-\top}\bigr),
$$
which is @eq-sandwich-asymptotic. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters, and the "bread"/"meat" nicknames.** When the model may be wrong, the MLE variance
$\mathcal I^{-1}$ is no longer correct; the right variance is the *sandwich*
$\mathbf A^{-1}\mathbf B\,\mathbf A^{-\top}$. The names are conventional and purely mnemonic, not
technical terms: $\mathbf A$ (the "bread") measures how *sensitive* the estimating equation is to the
parameter (the average slope of $\boldsymbol\psi$), while $\mathbf B$ (the "meat") measures how *variable*
the estimating equation itself is (the covariance of $\boldsymbol\psi$). The two outer copies of
$\mathbf A^{-1}$ are the bread, the central $\mathbf B$ is the meat; together they describe the shape
$\mathbf A^{-1}\,\mathbf B\,\mathbf A^{-\top}$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#def-sandwich-variance}
## Sandwich (robust) variance estimator
Under @thm-m-estimator-normal, the *sandwich variance estimator* of
$\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)$ is the empirical plug-in of @eq-sandwich-asymptotic,
$$
\widehat{\mathbb V}(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)
= \tfrac1n\,\widehat{\mathbf A}_n^{-1}\,\widehat{\mathbf B}_n\,\widehat{\mathbf A}_n^{-\top},
$$ {#eq-sandwich-estimator}
with
$$
\widehat{\mathbf A}_n = -\tfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\boldsymbol\psi(X_i; \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n),
\qquad
\widehat{\mathbf B}_n = \tfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \boldsymbol\psi(X_i; \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)\,\boldsymbol\psi(X_i; \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)^\top .
$$
The name records the structure $\widehat{\mathbf A}_n^{-1}$ (bread), $\widehat{\mathbf B}_n$ (meat),
$\widehat{\mathbf A}_n^{-\top}$ (bread). Under the regularity above, the law of large numbers and the
continuous mapping theorem give $\widehat{\mathbf A}_n \xrightarrow{p}\mathbf A(\boldsymbol\theta^{*})$
and $\widehat{\mathbf B}_n \xrightarrow{p}\mathbf B(\boldsymbol\theta^{*})$, so
$n\,\widehat{\mathbb V}(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) \xrightarrow{p}\mathbf A^{-1}\mathbf B\,\mathbf A^{-\top}$:
the sandwich estimator is consistent for the true asymptotic variance even when the working model is
misspecified. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation, with a picture.** The estimator is three matrices multiplied in a row: plug in the
empirical bread $\widehat{\mathbf A}_n$ and meat $\widehat{\mathbf B}_n$ computed from the data at the
fitted $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$, and you get a standard error valid even when the working model is
wrong.

```
                                A^{-1}        B          A^{-T}
   Var-hat(theta_hat)  =  (1/n) [ bread ] [  meat  ] [  bread  ]
                                sensitivity  variability  sensitivity
                                of the eqn   of the eqn   of the eqn
```

When the model is *right*, the information equality forces bread $=$ meat $= \mathcal I$ and the sandwich
collapses to $\mathcal I^{-1}$, the ordinary inverse-information variance (next corollary).
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The information equality is exactly the statement that, under correct specification, the sandwich
collapses to the familiar inverse-information variance.

::: {#cor-sandwich-collapse}
## Correct specification collapses the sandwich
Suppose $\boldsymbol\psi = \mathbf s$ is the score of a correctly specified regular model, so
$P = f(\cdot;\boldsymbol\theta_0)$ and $\boldsymbol\theta^{*} = \boldsymbol\theta_0$. Then
$\mathbf A(\boldsymbol\theta_0) = \mathbf B(\boldsymbol\theta_0) = \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)$, and the
sandwich variance @eq-sandwich-asymptotic reduces to $\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}$, recovering
@thm-mle-asymptotic-normality.
:::

::: {.proof}
The meat is $\mathbf B(\boldsymbol\theta_0) = \mathbb E[\mathbf s\,\mathbf s^\top] = \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)$
by @def-fisher-information. The bread is
$\mathbf A(\boldsymbol\theta_0) = -\mathbb E[\nabla\mathbf s] = -\mathbb E[\nabla^2 \ell] = \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)$
by the information equality (@thm-information-equality). Hence
$\mathbf A^{-1}\mathbf B\,\mathbf A^{-\top} = \mathcal I^{-1}\mathcal I\,\mathcal I^{-1} = \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}$.
$\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
## The sandwich and MAIC
When the model is misspecified, $\mathbf A \ne \mathbf B$ in general, and using the naive inverse-bread or
inverse-information variance understates (or overstates) the truth. The sandwich @eq-sandwich-estimator is
the universal fix.

This is the precise reason Chapter 18 reports robust standard errors for MAIC. In a matching-adjusted
indirect comparison the individual-level study fits weights
$w_i = \exp(\alpha + \boldsymbol\beta^\top \mathbf x_i)$ by an estimating equation that forces the weighted
covariate means to match the aggregate target population, schematically
$\sum_i w_i(\boldsymbol\beta)\,(\mathbf x_i - \bar{\mathbf x}^{*}) = \mathbf 0$; the treatment effect is
then estimated on the weighted sample. The "working model" here is the weighting scheme together with the
outcome model on the reweighted data, and there is no reason for it to be correctly specified: the weights
are a device for balancing covariates, not a belief about how the data arose. Maximum-likelihood
(inverse-information) standard errors would therefore be wrong, and only the sandwich form, with
$\boldsymbol\psi$ stacking the weighting equations and the outcome equation, is guaranteed consistent for
the sampling variance of the population-adjusted effect. Carry this picture into Chapter 18: weights solve
an estimating equation, the model is a working approximation, and the sandwich is the honest standard
error. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Tests and confidence intervals {#sec-tests}

We close with the three classical large-sample tests of a null hypothesis
$H_0 : \boldsymbol\theta = \boldsymbol\theta_0$ (or, after reparameterization, a value of a subvector),
and the confidence intervals obtained by inverting them. All three statistics have the same limiting
$\chi^2_p$ distribution and are first-order equivalent; they differ in whether they need the estimate, the
null value, or both. Throughout, $\mathcal I_n(\boldsymbol\theta) = n\,\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta)$ is the
sample information (@cor-information-additivity).

In a health application the practical question is which test to report for an indirect comparison. The
short answer: the three agree in large samples (@thm-wilks), but near a boundary or in small studies the
likelihood-ratio and score versions are usually preferred (see the remark after @thm-wilks). The table
contrasts what each test looks at.

| Test | What it evaluates | Needs the MLE $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$? | Needs the null fit? | Intuitive question |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wald | distance of $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$ from $\boldsymbol\theta_0$, scaled by curvature at $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$ | yes | no | "How many standard errors is the estimate from the null?" |
| Score (Rao) | slope of the log-likelihood evaluated at $\boldsymbol\theta_0$ | no | yes | "Is the log-likelihood still climbing steeply at the null?" |
| Likelihood ratio | drop in log-likelihood from $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$ down to $\boldsymbol\theta_0$ | yes | yes | "How much worse does the null fit than the best fit?" |

::: {#def-test-statistics}
## Wald, score, and likelihood-ratio statistics
For testing $H_0 : \boldsymbol\theta = \boldsymbol\theta_0$ with MLE $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$:

- the **Wald statistic** is
$$
W_n = (\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)^\top\, \mathcal I_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)\,(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0);
$$ {#eq-wald-stat}

- the **score (Rao) statistic** is
$$
R_n = \mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^\top\, \mathcal I_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0)^{-1}\, \mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0);
$$ {#eq-score-stat}

- the **likelihood-ratio statistic** is
$$
\Lambda_n = 2\bigl[\ell_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) - \ell_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0)\bigr] .
$$ {#eq-lr-stat}
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** All three compare a null value $\boldsymbol\theta_0$ to what the data prefer,
using the geometry of the log-likelihood near its peak (recall the parabola picture from the start of the
chapter). Wald measures the horizontal distance from the peak to the null; the score measures the slope at
the null; the likelihood ratio measures the vertical drop in height. Near the peak a smooth function looks
like a parabola, and for a parabola these three are the same measurement up to scaling, which is why
@thm-wilks finds them asymptotically equal. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#thm-wilks}
## Limiting null distribution (Wilks)
Under $H_0$ and the hypotheses of @thm-mle-asymptotic-normality, each of $W_n$, $R_n$, and $\Lambda_n$
converges in distribution to $\chi^2_p$, and the three are asymptotically equivalent:
$W_n - \Lambda_n \xrightarrow{p} 0$ and $R_n - \Lambda_n \xrightarrow{p} 0$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Abbreviate $\mathcal I = \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\theta_0)$ and let
$\mathbf Z_n = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0) \xrightarrow{d} \mathbf Z \sim \mathcal N_p(\mathbf 0, \mathcal I)$
by @eq-score-clt. From the proof of @thm-mle-asymptotic-normality,
$$
\sqrt n\,(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0) = \mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf Z_n + o_p(1).
$$ {#eq-mle-linearization}

**Score statistic.** Directly,
$R_n = \mathbf Z_n^\top (\tfrac1n \mathcal I_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0))^{-1}\mathbf Z_n = \mathbf Z_n^\top \mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf Z_n$,
and by continuous mapping (@thm-continuous-mapping) applied to the continuous map
$\mathbf z \mapsto \mathbf z^\top\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf z$,
$R_n \xrightarrow{d} \mathbf Z^\top \mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf Z$. Writing
$\mathbf Z = \mathcal I^{1/2}\mathbf G$ with $\mathbf G \sim \mathcal N_p(\mathbf 0, I_p)$ (the symmetric
PSD square root, @thm-cov-psd), $\mathbf Z^\top\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf Z = \mathbf G^\top\mathbf G = \|\mathbf G\|_2^2 \sim \chi^2_p$.
Hence $R_n \xrightarrow{d}\chi^2_p$.

**Wald statistic.** Since $\tfrac1n\mathcal I_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) = \mathcal I(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) \xrightarrow{p}\mathcal I$
(continuity of $\mathcal I$ and consistency), substituting @eq-mle-linearization,
$$
W_n = \bigl[\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)\bigr]^\top \mathcal I(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)\bigl[\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)\bigr]
= (\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf Z_n + o_p(1))^\top \mathcal I (\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf Z_n + o_p(1)) = \mathbf Z_n^\top\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf Z_n + o_p(1),
$$
using Slutsky to absorb the $o_p(1)$ terms (the leading factors are $O_p(1)$). Thus $W_n = R_n + o_p(1)$,
so $W_n \xrightarrow{d}\chi^2_p$ and $W_n - R_n \xrightarrow{p} 0$.

**Likelihood-ratio statistic.** Take a second-order Taylor expansion of $\ell_n$ about
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$, using $\mathbf s_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) = \mathbf 0$ and the integral
form of the remainder:
$$
\ell_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0) = \ell_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) + \mathbf 0 + \tfrac12 (\boldsymbol\theta_0 - \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)^\top \mathbf H_n(\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)(\boldsymbol\theta_0 - \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n),
$$
for $\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$ on the segment, so
$$
\Lambda_n = 2[\ell_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) - \ell_n(\boldsymbol\theta_0)]
= (\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)^\top\bigl[-\mathbf H_n(\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)\bigr](\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0).
$$
Now $-\tfrac1n \mathbf H_n(\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) \xrightarrow{p}\mathcal I$ (Step 4 of
@thm-mle-asymptotic-normality, since $\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p}\boldsymbol\theta_0$),
so $\Lambda_n = [\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)]^\top(-\tfrac1n\mathbf H_n)[\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)] = \mathbf Z_n^\top\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf Z_n + o_p(1)$
by the same substitution (both the averaged Hessian at $\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$ here and the one at
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n$ in the Wald step converge in probability to the same $\mathcal I$, because
$\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p}\boldsymbol\theta_0$ and
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p}\boldsymbol\theta_0$, and we substitute @eq-mle-linearization for
$\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta_0)$). Therefore $\Lambda_n = R_n + o_p(1) \xrightarrow{d}\chi^2_p$, and
$\Lambda_n - R_n \xrightarrow{p} 0$, $\Lambda_n - W_n \xrightarrow{p} 0$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters.** All three tests give the same answer in large samples, so for a single large
indirect comparison it rarely matters which you quote. What to remember: they are the three natural ways
to ask "is the effect different from the null," and a confidence interval is simply the set of null values
that none of them rejects (next remark). The picture is the parabola: the distance, slope, and height of a
parabola all encode the same curvature, which is why the statistics coincide. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
## Confidence intervals by inversion
A level-$\alpha$ test of $H_0 : \boldsymbol\theta = \boldsymbol\theta_0$ rejects when the statistic
exceeds the upper-$\alpha$ quantile $\chi^2_{p, 1-\alpha}$. The set of null values *not* rejected is a
$(1-\alpha)$ confidence region. For a scalar parameter the Wald region is the familiar interval
$$
\hat\theta_n \pm z_{1 - \alpha/2}\,\widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\hat\theta_n),
\qquad \widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\hat\theta_n) = \bigl(\mathcal I_n(\hat\theta_n)\bigr)^{-1/2},
$$
where $z_{1-\alpha/2} = \Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha/2)$ and $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function
([Notation](/notation.qmd)). Inverting the likelihood-ratio test instead gives the *profile-likelihood* interval
$\{\theta : 2[\ell_n(\hat\theta_n) - \ell_n(\theta)] \le \chi^2_{1, 1-\alpha}\}$, which respects the shape
of the log-likelihood and is not forced to be symmetric. The three intervals agree to first order by
@thm-wilks but can differ markedly in small samples or near a boundary, where the likelihood-ratio and
score intervals are generally preferred. Concretely, to build a confidence interval by hand you can sweep
candidate null values $\theta_0$, run the test at each, and keep those it does *not* reject; the retained
values form the interval. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## A fully worked example {#sec-worked-example}

We tie the chapter together on the simplest nontrivial model, the Bernoulli, where every quantity can be
computed by hand, and then illustrate the sandwich variance on a deliberately misspecified model. Most
pieces have already appeared in context, threaded through the running example: the score in
@lem-score-mean-zero, the information in @cor-information-additivity, the log-odds delta method in
@exm-delta-logodds, and the indirect comparison in @exm-indirect-bucher. Here we assemble them on the one
dataset $n = 25$, $\sum_i X_i = 10$.

::: {#exm-binomial-inference}
## Maximum likelihood for a Bernoulli proportion
Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be iid $\mathrm{Ber}(p)$ with $\theta = p \in (0,1)$. Suppose we observe $n = 25$
trials with $\sum_i X_i = 10$ successes.

**Likelihood, score, MLE.** The single-observation density is $f(x; p) = p^x(1-p)^{1-x}$, so
$$
\ell_n(p) = \Bigl(\textstyle\sum_i X_i\Bigr)\log p + \Bigl(n - \textstyle\sum_i X_i\Bigr)\log(1-p) = 10\log p + 15\log(1-p)
$$
(dropping the constant binomial coefficient, which does not depend on $p$). The score is
$$
s_n(p) = \frac{10}{p} - \frac{15}{1-p}, \qquad s_n(p) = 0 \iff 10(1-p) = 15 p \iff \hat p = \tfrac{10}{25} = 0.40 .
$$
This matches @def-mle: $\hat p_{\mathrm{MLE}} = \bar X_n$.

**Fisher information and standard error.** The per-observation score is $s(p; x) = x/p - (1-x)/(1-p)$,
and by the information equality (@thm-information-equality), with
$\partial_p^2 \log f = -x/p^2 - (1-x)/(1-p)^2$ and $\mathbb E[X] = p$,
$$
\mathcal I(p) = -\mathbb E_p\bigl[\partial_p^2 \log f\bigr] = \frac{p}{p^2} + \frac{1-p}{(1-p)^2} = \frac1p + \frac{1}{1-p} = \frac{1}{p(1-p)} .
$$
At $\hat p = 0.4$, $\mathcal I(\hat p) = 1/(0.4\cdot 0.6) = 1/0.24 = 4.1\overline{6}$, the sample
information is $\mathcal I_n(\hat p) = 25 \times 4.1\overline 6 = 104.1\overline 6$, and the asymptotic
variance of $\hat p$ is
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat p) = \frac{1}{\mathcal I_n(\hat p)} = \frac{\hat p(1 - \hat p)}{n} = \frac{0.24}{25} = 0.0096,
\qquad \widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\hat p) = \sqrt{0.0096} = 0.09798 .
$$
The Wald 95% confidence interval (@sec-tests) is
$0.40 \pm 1.96 \times 0.09798 = 0.40 \pm 0.19204 = (0.2080,\, 0.5920)$.

**Delta method for the log-odds.** The log-odds is $g(p) = \log\!\frac{p}{1-p}$ with
$g'(p) = \frac{1}{p(1-p)}$. By the delta method (@thm-delta-method),
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}\bigl(g(\hat p)\bigr) = g'(\hat p)^2\,\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat p)
= \Bigl(\frac{1}{p(1-p)}\Bigr)^2 \cdot \frac{p(1-p)}{n} = \frac{1}{n\,p(1-p)}\Big|_{p = \hat p} = \frac{1}{25 \times 0.24} = \frac16 = 0.1\overline 6 .
$$
Notice the algebra collapses to $\tfrac{1}{n\hat p(1-\hat p)} = \tfrac{1}{n\hat p} + \tfrac{1}{n(1-\hat p)} = \tfrac{1}{\#\text{success}} + \tfrac{1}{\#\text{fail}} = \tfrac{1}{10} + \tfrac{1}{15} = 0.1\overline 6$,
the textbook standard error of an empirical log-odds. Thus $g(\hat p) = \log(0.4/0.6) = -0.40546$ with
$\widehat{\mathrm{se}} = \sqrt{1/6} = 0.40825$, giving a 95% interval for the log-odds of
$-0.40546 \pm 1.96 \times 0.40825 = (-1.2056,\, 0.3947)$ and, exponentiating, an odds-ratio-scale
interval $(e^{-1.2056}, e^{0.3947}) = (0.2995,\, 1.4830)$.

**Three tests of $H_0 : p = 0.5$.** Using @def-test-statistics with $\boldsymbol\theta_0 = 0.5$:

- *Score test.* $s_n(0.5) = 10/0.5 - 15/0.5 = -10$ and $\mathcal I_n(0.5) = 25/(0.5\cdot 0.5) = 100$, so
$R_n = (-10)^2/100 = 1.000$.

- *Wald test.* $W_n = (\hat p - 0.5)^2\,\mathcal I_n(\hat p) = (-0.1)^2 \times 104.1\overline 6 = 0.01/0.0096 = 1.0417$.

- *Likelihood-ratio test.* $\ell_n(0.4) = 10\log 0.4 + 15\log 0.6 = -9.16291 - 7.66238 = -16.82529$ and
$\ell_n(0.5) = 25\log 0.5 = -17.32868$, so
$\Lambda_n = 2(-16.82529 + 17.32868) = 2 \times 0.50339 = 1.0068$.

All three statistics cluster near $1.0$, confirming the first-order equivalence of @thm-wilks. Against
the critical value $\chi^2_{1, 0.95} = 3.841$, none rejects $H_0 : p = 0.5$; equivalently, $0.5$ lies
inside the Wald interval $(0.208, 0.592)$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#exm-sandwich-normal}
## When the model is wrong: the sandwich earns its name
Suppose we estimate a population mean $\mu$ by fitting a *working* model that treats the data as
$\mathcal N(\mu, 1)$ with the variance fixed (incorrectly) at $1$, while the true distribution $P$ has
mean $\mu_0$ and variance $\sigma_0^2 \ne 1$. The working score is
$\psi(x; \mu) = \partial_\mu\bigl[-\tfrac12(x - \mu)^2\bigr] = x - \mu$, so the estimating equation
$\sum_i (X_i - \hat\mu_n) = 0$ yields the M-estimator $\hat\mu_n = \bar X_n$, which targets
$\mu^{*} = \mu_0$.

By @thm-m-estimator-normal, the bread and meat are
$$
\mathbf A = -\mathbb E_P[\partial_\mu \psi] = -\mathbb E_P[-1] = 1,
\qquad
\mathbf B = \mathbb E_P[\psi^2] = \mathbb E_P[(X - \mu_0)^2] = \sigma_0^2,
$$
so the correct asymptotic variance is $\mathbf A^{-1}\mathbf B\,\mathbf A^{-1}/n = \sigma_0^2/n$, exactly
the variance of $\bar X_n$. The naive model-based variance, which trusts the working model and uses the
inverse working information $\mathbf A^{-1}/n = 1/n$, is wrong by the factor $\sigma_0^2$.

**Concrete numbers.** Take $n = 40$ observations with sample mean $\bar X_n = 2.5$ and
$\sum_i (X_i - \bar X_n)^2 = 160$. Then
$\widehat{\mathbf A}_n = 1$, $\widehat{\mathbf B}_n = 160/40 = 4.0$, and the sandwich variance
@eq-sandwich-estimator is
$$
\widehat{\mathbb V}(\hat\mu_n) = \tfrac1n\,\widehat{\mathbf A}_n^{-1}\,\widehat{\mathbf B}_n\,\widehat{\mathbf A}_n^{-1} = \frac{4.0}{40} = 0.10,
\qquad \widehat{\mathrm{se}}_{\text{robust}} = \sqrt{0.10} = 0.3162,
$$
whereas the naive standard error is $\sqrt{1/40} = 0.1581$, understating the true uncertainty by a
factor of $\sqrt{\widehat{\mathbf B}_n} = 2$. This is the mechanism, in miniature, that makes the
sandwich estimator mandatory for MAIC in Chapter 18: the weighting "model" is a computational device, not
a believed truth, and only the robust variance is consistent. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Notes and references {#sec-notes}

The estimation theory of this chapter is classical and is developed, with the regression emphasis this
book shares, in @bingham2010regression; the worked Bernoulli example and the three-test comparison follow
that source's treatment of likelihood inference. The notation for likelihood, score, Fisher information,
the MLE, and the sandwich variance matches [Notation](/notation.qmd).

The asymptotic tools of @sec-asymptotic-tools correspond to the proof catalogue: the delta method is
A.11, Slutsky's theorem is A.12, and the continuous mapping theorem is A.13 (corresponds to A.11-A.13 in
the proof catalogue). Our statements and proofs align with the companion manuscript's treatment in
`manuscript/01_probability.md`; we have expanded the catalogue's one-line sketches into full proofs and
have generalized the delta method and Slutsky's theorem to the multivariate case via the Cramér-Wold
device. The continuous mapping and Slutsky proofs rest on the Portmanteau theorem, which we cite as a
standard result of weak-convergence theory.

The consistency proof (@thm-mle-consistency) is the Wald argmax argument: the Kullback-Leibler
information inequality (@lem-kl-information-inequality, a consequence of Jensen's inequality
@thm-jensen) identifies $\boldsymbol\theta_0$ as the unique maximizer of the population log-likelihood,
a uniform law of large numbers (@lem-uniform-lln, cited) transfers this to the sample, and the
argmax-continuity lemma (@lem-argmax-consistency, proved in full) concludes. The asymptotic-normality
proof (@thm-mle-asymptotic-normality) is the standard Taylor expansion of the score, assembled from the
information equality (@thm-information-equality), the multivariate central limit theorem, and Slutsky's
theorem, with the affine-image property of the multivariate normal (@thm-mvn-linear from Chapter 4)
delivering the Gaussian limit. The Cramér-Rao bound (@thm-cramer-rao) is proved via the covariance
Cauchy-Schwarz inequality (@thm-cauchy-schwarz-ip), with the matrix version following from
positive-semidefiniteness of a joint covariance (@thm-cov-psd) and a Schur-complement computation.

M-estimation and the sandwich variance (@def-sandwich-variance) generalize maximum likelihood; the
collapse of the sandwich to the inverse information under correct specification (@cor-sandwich-collapse)
is a direct corollary of the information equality, and is the conceptual bridge to the robust variance
used for MAIC in Chapter 18. The convolution-theorem justification of asymptotic efficiency is cited, not
proved, as it requires the local asymptotic normality machinery outside the scope of a foundations
chapter.

No result in this chapter is tagged machine-checked. The companion Coq development depends on
`mathcomp-analysis` for measure-theoretic foundations and, per the manuscript, treats the asymptotic
results A.11-A.13 at the level of cited library facts rather than re-derived theorems; the
pen-and-paper proofs here are the authoritative versions. Candidates for future formalization are the
information equality and the M-estimator sandwich, both of which are purely algebraic given the
differentiation-under-the-integral hypotheses.

## Exercises {#sec-exercises}

The exercises progress from warm-ups and interpretation to computation and proof. A starred exercise
($\star$) has a full worked solution in Appendix F; the first warm-up below is solved inline so you can
calibrate your approach before attempting the rest.

::: {#exr-warmup-2x2}
## Warm-up (solved): a log odds and its interval from one arm
In a single-arm cohort, $20$ of $50$ patients respond. (a) Give the MLE $\hat p$. (b) Give the log odds
$g(\hat p) = \log\frac{\hat p}{1 - \hat p}$ and its delta-method standard error. (c) Report a 95%
confidence interval on the log-odds scale and on the odds scale.

*Solution.* (a) $\hat p = 20/50 = 0.40$. (b) The log odds is
$g(\hat p) = \log(0.40/0.60) = \log(0.6667) = -0.4055$. By @exm-delta-logodds the variance of an empirical
log odds is $\tfrac{1}{\#\text{responders}} + \tfrac{1}{\#\text{non-responders}} = \tfrac1{20} + \tfrac1{30} = 0.08333$,
so the standard error is $\sqrt{0.08333} = 0.2887$. (c) On the log-odds scale,
$-0.4055 \pm 1.96 \times 0.2887 = (-0.9713,\, 0.1603)$; exponentiating gives the odds-scale interval
$(e^{-0.9713}, e^{0.1603}) = (0.379,\, 1.174)$. The interval includes odds $1$ (probability $0.5$), so the
data are consistent with a coin-flip response rate. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#exr-interpret-information}
## Warm-up (interpretation): where is a proportion hardest to estimate?
Using $\mathcal I(p) = 1/[p(1 - p)]$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\hat p) \approx p(1 - p)/n$: (a) for fixed $n$, at
what value of $p$ is $\hat p$ most variable, and where is it most precise? (b) A trial wants the standard
error of $\hat p$ below $0.02$ when the true $p$ is near $0.5$; roughly how many patients are needed?
(c) In one sentence, relate your answer to why the Fisher information is largest near $p = 0$ or $p = 1$.
:::

::: {#exr-indirect-se}
## Interpretation: the cost of going indirect
In @exm-indirect-bucher the direct contrasts had standard errors $0.456$ and $0.410$, while the indirect
contrast of $B$ versus $C$ had standard error $0.614$. (a) Show that the indirect variance is the sum of
the two direct variances and confirm the number. (b) Explain in one sentence why an indirect comparison is
necessarily less precise than the direct comparisons it is built from. (c) If a third trial directly
compared $B$ and $C$ with standard error $0.30$, which estimate would you trust more, and why?
:::

::: {#exr-poisson-mle}
## Poisson information and efficiency
Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be iid $\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)$. (a) Derive the MLE $\hat\lambda_n$. (b) Compute the
score, show it has mean zero, and compute the Fisher information $\mathcal I(\lambda)$ two ways (as the
variance of the score and as minus the expected second derivative), confirming the information equality.
(c) Show $\hat\lambda_n$ is unbiased and attains the Cramér-Rao bound exactly, hence is efficient.
:::

::: {#exr-exponential-rate}
## Reparameterization and invariance
Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be iid Exponential with rate $\lambda > 0$, density $f(x;\lambda) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}$
on $x > 0$. (a) Find the MLE of $\lambda$. (b) Using invariance (@prp-mle-invariance), write down the MLE
of the mean $\eta = 1/\lambda$ and of the median $m = (\log 2)/\lambda$. (c) Use the delta method
(@thm-delta-method) to give the asymptotic variance of $\hat\eta_n$, and verify it equals the Cramér-Rao
bound for estimating $\eta$.
:::

::: {#exr-mse-shrinkage}
## Bias can lower MSE
For iid $\mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ data with known $\sigma^2$, consider the shrinkage estimator
$\hat\mu_c = c\,\bar X_n$ for a constant $c \in [0,1]$. (a) Using @prp-bias-variance-decomposition, write
$\mathrm{MSE}_\mu(\hat\mu_c)$ as a function of $c$. (b) Minimize over $c$ and show the optimal $c^{*}$ is
strictly less than $1$ whenever $\mu \ne 0$, so a biased estimator strictly beats the unbiased
$\bar X_n$ in MSE. (c) Explain why this does not contradict the Cramér-Rao bound.
:::

::: {#exr-score-test-binomial}
## Score versus Wald in finite samples
Repeat the three tests of @exm-binomial-inference for the data $n = 25$, $\sum_i X_i = 10$ against the
null $H_0 : p = 0.3$. Report $W_n$, $R_n$, and $\Lambda_n$ to three decimals and state which (if any)
reject at level $0.05$. Comment on the ordering $W_n$, $R_n$, $\Lambda_n$ you observe.
:::

::: {#exr-information-equality-fail}
## Where the information equality fails ($\star$)
The information equality (@thm-information-equality) requires regularity (@def-regular-model), in
particular a common support not depending on the parameter. Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be iid
Uniform$(0, \theta)$, whose support $(0, \theta)$ does depend on $\theta$. (a) Show that the naive score
$\partial_\theta \log f = -1/\theta$ has nonzero expectation, so @lem-score-mean-zero fails. (b) Show the
MLE is $\hat\theta_n = \max_i X_i$, that $n(\theta - \hat\theta_n)/\theta \xrightarrow{d} \mathrm{Exp}(1)$,
and hence the rate is $n$ rather than $\sqrt n$ and the limit is not normal. (c) Explain precisely which
hypotheses of @thm-mle-asymptotic-normality are violated. *(Solution in Appendix F.)*
:::

::: {#exr-sandwich-derivation}
## Sandwich variance for a misspecified Poisson ($\star$)
Suppose the true data are overdispersed counts with mean $\mu_0$ and variance
$v_0 = \kappa\,\mu_0$ for some $\kappa > 1$ (so $\kappa = 1$ would be Poisson), but we fit a working
Poisson model with log-likelihood contribution $x\log\mu - \mu$. (a) Show the working score is
$\psi(x;\mu) = x/\mu - 1$ and the M-estimator is $\hat\mu_n = \bar X_n$, targeting $\mu^{*} = \mu_0$.
(b) Compute the bread $\mathbf A(\mu_0)$ and meat $\mathbf B(\mu_0)$ and show the sandwich asymptotic
variance is $\kappa\,\mu_0/n$, whereas the naive model-based variance is $\mu_0/n$. (c) Conclude that the
naive Poisson standard error understates the truth by the factor $\sqrt\kappa$, and relate this to
@cor-sandwich-collapse. *(Solution in Appendix F.)*
:::

::: {#exr-delta-multivariate}
## Multivariate delta method for a ratio
Let $(\hat\alpha_n, \hat\beta_n)$ be jointly asymptotically normal,
$\sqrt n\bigl((\hat\alpha_n, \hat\beta_n) - (\alpha, \beta)\bigr) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N_2(\mathbf 0, \boldsymbol\Sigma)$
with $\boldsymbol\Sigma = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} \sigma_\alpha^2 & \sigma_{\alpha\beta} \\ \sigma_{\alpha\beta} & \sigma_\beta^2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$
and $\beta \ne 0$. Using @thm-delta-method, derive the asymptotic variance of the ratio
$\hat\rho_n = \hat\alpha_n / \hat\beta_n$. Specialize to the independent case
$\sigma_{\alpha\beta} = 0$ and comment on the well-known instability when $\beta$ is near zero.
:::
